{"title":"Read models on another database handle are not fenced against a purge and can write a row for a purged document from a batch fetched just before the purge committed","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T19:30:27.633Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T19:30:27.633Z","description":"Models on the reactor's database wait for a purge and it waits for them; external ones (attachment reference index, relational processors) only skip purged ids. Repair: rescan from markerOrdinal − 1."}

{"content":"## The failure

Erasure removes a document from read models only where it can coordinate with them. Read models whose tables are on the **reactor's own database** are fenced: a purge waits for them and they wait for a purge, so no row survives. Read models whose rows live on **another database handle**, such as the attachment reference index or a third-party relational processor, cannot share the purge's transaction. They skip ids that are already purged when they fetch, but a batch fetched just before the purge committed can still be written after it. The result is a row about an erased document that nothing will remove.

## Detection and repair

The marker's ordinal bounds the window. `markerOrdinal` appears on the erasure item (`erasureRequest`) and in the `purged` audit row. Rescanning the affected read model from just below it removes the straggler:

```bash
# from packages/reactor of the monorepo
pnpm catchup rescan --pg <url> --from <markerOrdinal - 1> --consumer <read-model-id>
```

## Conditions

- Only out-of-database read models are exposed; the reactor's fenced models and the privacy add-on's own subject index (a fenced read model over the reactor handle) are not.
- The page offers no automatic sweep, so an operator running external processors should rescan after every completed erasure.
- Erasure as a whole has a wider boundary than read models (see "Reactor erasure stops at the reactor's own storage ...").

## Evidence

Academy › Reference › Reactor › Document erasure, "Read models on another database". Code at e0f277d: `packages/reactor/src/read-models/base-read-model.ts` and `processors/processor-manager.ts` import `findPurged` to skip purged ids, which is the skip-not-fence behaviour described.

{"content":"The v6 Reactor replaced `onStrands(strands: InternalTransmitterUpdate[])` with `onOperations(operations: OperationWithContext[])`. Each item destructures as `{ operation, context }`. `context` carries `documentId`, `documentType`, `scope`, `branch`, the global `ordinal`, and an optional `resultingState` (a JSON string). `operation` carries `action` (`type`, `input`, `timestampUtcMs`, `id`, `scope`), `index`, `timestampUtcMs` and `hash`. Field access moves with it: `operation.type` → `operation.action.type`, `operation.input` → `operation.action.input`, `operation.timestamp` → `operation.action.timestampUtcMs`.

Strands carried `driveId`; the flat context does not. The drive id now reaches a processor through its factory: the inner factory function takes `(driveHeader: PHDocumentHeader, processorApp?: ProcessorApp)` instead of `(driveId: string)`, and the outer one takes the `IProcessorHostModule` instead of direct dependencies. The relational factory passes `driveHeader.id` to the processor's constructor as a fourth argument for exactly this reason.

## What the flat list does not promise
`ordinal` is a global counter, but the list is **not** delivered in global ordinal order. Within one document's scope and branch, operations arrive in ordinal order; across documents a call can carry an ordinal lower than one an earlier call carried, because batches reach the manager one document at a time and documents are projected in parallel. Delivery is at-least-once: a restart, `tracked.retry()` (which replays from the processor's cursor), or a backfill that reads an operation whose live batch is still on its way can hand a processor the same operation again. The migration guide's own advice that "each operation is delivered exactly once — there is no replay", so `clearSource` guards can be dropped, is therefore wrong at this version: keep writes idempotent (upserts, dedup keys).

Backfill still pages through `operationIndex.getSinceOrdinal(lastOrdinal)` when a factory registers against a drive with history, after a restart, and on `retry()`. Cursors persist in the `ProcessorCursor` table keyed by `processorId`.

Checked against the `IProcessor.onOperations` contract in `packages/shared/processors/types.ts` at e0f277d.

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T19:32:07.662Z","description":"Extend RelationalDbProcessor<DB> for a typed this.relationalDb, getNamespace(driveId) isolation, initAndUpgrade() migrations, and erasure helpers that need the drive id passed as a fourth argument."}

{"content":"The v6 Reactor provides `RelationalDbProcessor<DB>` as a base class for processors that need database access. What it gives you:

- `static getNamespace(driveId)` — per-drive database isolation, defaulting to `${this.name}_${driveId.replaceAll("-","_")}`; override it to choose another namespace.
- `initAndUpgrade()` — the lifecycle hook where the processor runs its own migrations (`await up(this.relationalDb)`).
- `this.relationalDb` — a typed Kysely instance on the namespace the factory opened.
- `static query(driveId, relationalDb)` — a read-only query builder on that namespace, for subgraphs.
- Erasure helpers — `deleteDocumentRows`, `isNamespaceDrive` and `dropNamespace` — for a deleted document's rows and a deleted drive's namespace.

The factory opens the namespace with `module.relationalDb.createNamespace<T>(namespace)` and constructs the processor with `(namespace, filter, store, driveHeader.id)`. The fourth argument is optional in the constructor (`_driveId?: string`) but not in practice: it is what `isNamespaceDrive` compares a deleted document's id against, so a processor built without it never drops its namespace on its drive's deletion. Codegen's relational factory template passes it.

Scaffolding: `ph generate processor --name <name> --type relationalDb --document-types <type>` (the migration guide's `ph generate --processor … --processor-type …` form is out of date; the CLI at e0f277d takes the `processor` subcommand with `--name`, `--type`, `--document-types`).

Checked against `packages/shared/processors/relational/types.ts` and `packages/codegen/src/templates/processors/relational-db/factory.ts` at e0f277d.

_Corrected 2026-08-13 against Powerhouse v6.2.2-dev.45._

## Correction at v6.2.2-dev.74
"Lifecycle management" overstates what the base class does about migrations. At v6.2.2-dev.74 the generated template makes migrations the processor's own responsibility:

```ts
export class MyProcessor extends RelationalDbProcessor<DB> {
  override async initAndUpgrade(): Promise<void> { await up(this.relationalDb); }
}
```

So there is no automatic discovery of a migrations folder — `initAndUpgrade` is the hook, and the processor calls its own `up`. Per-drive namespace isolation and the type-safe Kysely surface are unchanged.

## Revision history
- v6.2.3-dev.91+e0f277d (2026-11-03): the constructor gained an optional fourth argument, the drive id, and the base class gained `deleteDocumentRows`, `isNamespaceDrive` and `dropNamespace`. The migration guide's relational factory now passes `driveHeader.id` (e2aee31028), because deletion matching moved from the namespace to the drive id (78175ef110 "match a relational processor's own drive by id, not namespace").","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T19:32:07.662Z"}

{"title":"Processor deliveries are ordered only within one document's scope and branch, so a processor cannot rely on a referenced document having arrived first","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T19:37:40.320Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T19:37:40.320Z","description":"Documents are projected in parallel and reach the manager one at a time; sort a call by context.ordinal if needed, but resolve cross-document references from your own store."}

{"content":"## The claim
A processor cannot assume operations reach it in global ordinal order. Within one document's scope and branch they arrive in ordinal order; across documents a call can carry an ordinal lower than one an earlier call carried. So when an operation on document X refers to document Y, Y's creation can reach the processor after the operation that refers to it.

## Why
Batches reach the processor manager one document at a time, and different documents are projected in parallel: each projection chain runs its own pre-ready, `READ_READY`, post-ready sequence. Each processor then has its own delivery queue, and batches that queue up behind a running call are merged into the next call in the order they arrived. Arrival order across documents is whatever order the parallel chains finished in. The `ordinal` on `context` is still a global counter, which is why it looks like an ordering guarantee when it is not one.

The `IProcessor.onOperations` contract in `packages/shared/processors/types.ts` at e0f277d says so directly: within a document's scope and branch each call is in ordinal order, "and an operation delivered late comes with every later operation of its stream this processor was already given. Across documents there is no ordering guarantee."

## What to do
- Need ordinal order inside one call? Sort the batch by `context.ordinal` at the top of `onOperations`. No ordering is available across calls.
- Resolving a reference to another document: look it up in the read model or relational store the processor already writes, and handle "not there yet" (keep the reference pending, or write a row the later operation completes) rather than relying on arrival order.
- A consequence (an inference from the contract, not stated by the docs): a per-document "last ordinal seen" is a safe dedup key; one global high-water mark used to skip "old" operations is not, because a lower ordinal can legitimately arrive later.

## Conditions
Holds at v6.2.3-dev.91+e0f277d for live routing and for live batches mixed with backfill. Before the queue-based delivery contract (reactor commit d968ebef99, 2026-09-23) the docs described steady-state live routing as globally ordered; "V6 processors receive a flat OperationWithContext list via onOperations instead of grouped strands via onStrands" carried that claim and was corrected in place.

## Evidence

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T19:39:37.663Z","description":"Placement matters: the same processor code that would burden a browser runs server-side, turning append-only operations into queryable projections."}

{"content":"Processors are the third kind of code in a Powerhouse package, and Switchboard is where they execute.

Evidence: "This is where processors run in the background, where read models are maintained" and "Switchboard runs your processors, which fold the operation stream into read models and expose them over GraphQL."

Mechanism: a processor subscribes to the operation stream, folds it into a derived projection, and the host serves that projection over GraphQL. Because the input is the append-only log, a read model can be rebuilt by replaying from the beginning rather than repaired in place.

When it holds: only where a server-side Reactor exists. Connect embeds a Reactor but does not run processors, so a browser-only deployment has no read models.

What it lets a reader predict: expensive aggregation belongs in a processor, never in an editor component, and a corrupted read model is fixed by replay, not by a migration.","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T19:39:37.663Z"}

{"title":"Subgraphs are modular components that extend document models with custom GraphQL queries, plain HTTP routes, external integrations and cross-document logic","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T19:42:49.693Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T19:42:49.693Z","description":"Generated with ph generate subgraph --name <name>: a schema plus resolvers reading through ctx.clients, joined into the supergraph, optionally with HTTP routes and webhooks under its namespace."}

{"content":"A subgraph is an independent service unit with its own GraphQL schema and resolvers. It can connect to external APIs, add custom queries and mutations, automate interactions between document models, and read from the Reactor, relational data stores (processor namespaces) and analytics stores. It consists of a schema (types, queries, mutations), resolvers (data fetching and logic) and context fields (auth, external sources).

Generated with `ph generate subgraph --name <name>`, a subgraph auto-registers at `/graphql/<name>`. The supergraph gateway at `/graphql` combines all subgraphs (except the drive subgraph at `/d/:driveId`) into one endpoint, so one request can query document models and custom subgraphs together.

**How resolvers reach the Reactor.** A resolver reads through `ctx.clients.read`, the read half of the reactor client that the GraphQL layer puts on each request's context, and writes through `ctx.clients.write`, which exists only while a mutation executes. Setup-time code (schema building, model lookup) uses `this.readClient`. `subgraph.reactorClient` survives as a `@deprecated` facade over both halves for subgraphs that have not moved. Attachments come from `this.attachmentsFor(ctx)`, a client bound to the request's caller.

**Not only GraphQL.** The same subgraph can serve plain HTTP endpoints under the package's own namespace through `this.http`, and inbound provider webhooks through `this.http.webhooks`.

Authorization stays the subgraph's job: a custom resolver runs with full access to the Reactor, so guarding reads, writes and document creation is the author's responsibility.

Checked against `packages/reactor-api/src/graphql/base-subgraph.ts` at e0f277d (`readClient`, deprecated `reactorClient`, `http`, `attachmentsFor`, `clientsOf`).

_Corrected 2026-08-13 against Powerhouse v6.2.2-dev.45._

{"title":"A subgraph resolver gets a write client only while a mutation executes: ctx.clients.write in a query or subscription throws WriteClientUnavailableError","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T19:43:28.352Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T19:43:28.352Z","description":"The GraphQL layer binds the reactor client's read and write halves per operation, so query resolvers cannot write by construction; a few write-side queries are bound explicitly."}

{"content":"## The claim
The GraphQL layer puts the reactor client on each request's context split by operation type. `ctx.clients.read` is always there; `ctx.clients.write` exists only while the executing operation is a mutation. Touching `ctx.clients.write` in a query or a subscription throws `WriteClientUnavailableError` ("ctx.clients.write is only available to Mutation fields; field X runs in a query. Read through ctx.clients.read."). A context the GraphQL layer never bound, such as a resolver called directly from a test, gets the read half and a write that refuses.

## Why it is built this way
ADR 0006 (reactor client halves) split `IReactorClient` into a read half and a write half, so that queries never depend on write-side state and mutations resolve their targets without the read model. The rule "queries read, mutations write" could have been a lint rule; that was rejected because third-party subgraphs are not linted by the monorepo. Gating the context catches them at runtime, with an error that names the field.

## Mechanism
`RequestClientBinder` wraps each subgraph's resolver map, so every resolver receives a context derived for its own operation, memoized per request and operation so all fields of one operation see the same object. The refusing `write` property is not enumerable, so spreading or logging `ctx.clients` does not trip it. A few reactor-subgraph queries serve write-side state by design (sync polling and holds, `evaluateActions`); they are bound explicitly through `WRITE_SIDE_QUERIES` and receive both halves.

## Conditions and consequences
- The gate applies to `ctx.clients`. `subgraph.reactorClient` survives as a `@deprecated` facade over both halves, so a subgraph that has not moved can still write from a query; the rule bites only code that adopts `ctx.clients`.
- A mutation resolver writes through the write half, gets a handle, and reads back once with the receipt's consistency token.
- Moving a custom resolver from `subgraph.reactorClient` to `ctx.clients` therefore also moves any write it makes into a mutation field.

## Evidence
Academy › Build › WorkWithData › Using subgraphs, the `searchTodos` resolver sample ("Resolvers read through ctx.clients.read; ctx.clients.write exists only in mutations"). {"content":"A processor implements `IProcessor` with `onOperations(operations: OperationWithContext[])` and `onDisconnect()`. Each `OperationWithContext` pairs an `Operation` (action type, input, index, hash, timestamp) with an `OperationContext` (documentId, documentType, scope, branch, `ordinal`, and `resultingState` as JSON). The `ordinal` is a global counter, but delivery is ordered only within one document's scope and branch, not across documents.

`ProcessorFilter` has optional arrays: `documentType`, `scope`, `branch`, `documentId`. A field that is `undefined` or `[]` matches everything; a field with values matches when the operation's context value is in the array; all present fields must match. The `"*"` wildcard is honored **only in `documentId`** — in `documentType`, `scope`, and `branch` a literal `"*"` matches only an operation whose value is the string `"*"`, i.e. nothing real. To match all scopes, omit `scope` or set it to `[]`; never write `scope: ["*"]`.

The scopes a filter names decide which lifecycle events a processor sees: `["global"]` carries shared state, `["local"]` user-specific state, and `["document"]` the document lifecycle operations such as `DELETE_DOCUMENT` and `PURGE_DOCUMENT`. A processor that stores data needs `"document"` in its scope to erase a deleted document's rows.

The factory pattern: the outer function receives `IProcessorHostModule` (shared resources), the inner function receives the drive's `driveHeader` once per drive, and returns `ProcessorRecord[]`. By default processors replay all history; set `startFrom: "current"` to skip it. `onDisconnect()` runs when the processor is disconnected — when its drive is deleted, and also when its factory is unregistered or reloaded, so it is cleanup, not a deletion signal.

Checked against `packages/shared/processors/types.ts` and `packages/reactor/src/processors/utils.ts` (`matchesFilter`) at e0f277d.

Dropped the remark that the codegen analytics template emits `scope: ["*"]`: at e0f277d it omits `scope`.","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T19:49:04.326Z"}

{"title":"A processor factory is invoked only once a drive container exists, so until a drive is created no operation reaches any processor","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T19:51:34.628Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T19:51:34.628Z","description":"The manager calls factories on a CREATE_DOCUMENT of a drive container type (powerhouse/document-drive or reactor-drive by default); plain documents matching a filter are not routed first."}

{"content":"## The claim
Processors are per drive. The processor manager calls a registered factory when it sees a `CREATE_DOCUMENT` whose document type is a drive container, or when a factory registers against drives that already exist. Until a drive exists, a registered factory is never invoked and no operation is routed — even operations on plain documents that match a processor's filter.

The container types default to `powerhouse/document-drive` and `powerhouse/reactor-drive` (`DEFAULT_DRIVE_CONTAINER_TYPES` in `packages/reactor/src/core/drive-container-types.ts`) and are set with the reactor builder's `withDriveContainerTypes(types)`.

## Why it matters
In a standalone reactor (a test, a script, a recipe) it is easy to create documents, register a processor and wonder why `onOperations` never fires: with no drive there is no processor instance to call. Create a drive before you expect deliveries. The same holds for a custom drive-like container: by implication, its processors are created only if its type is in the container set.

## Where it sits
This is the step before everything in "Processors implement IProcessor with onOperations…": the factory that produces per-drive instances runs only when a drive appears. It also explains why `ProcessorFactory` takes a drive header rather than a document.

{"title":"A factory registered after its drive exists still receives the drive's creation header, so slug- or name-selecting factories work after a restart; only a purged drive's header is minimal","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T19:51:40.149Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T19:51:40.149Z","description":"The manager rebuilds the header from the drive's CREATE_DOCUMENT in the operation index, a few drives at a time; earlier releases passed a late registration only id and documentType."}

{"content":"## The claim
`ProcessorFactory` receives a `PHDocumentHeader`, and that header is the drive's header **as it was created**, from its `CREATE_DOCUMENT`. That holds for a drive created while the factory is registered (taken from the routed batch) and for one that already existed when `registerFactory` is called, after a restart or a package reload: the manager rebuilds the header from the action input in the operation index, which keeps no `resultingState`, reading a late registration's headers a few drives at a time. Earlier releases passed a late registration a minimal header with only `id` and `documentType` set.

## Why it matters
A factory that selects drives by `slug` or `name` (vetra's codegen factory does) used to make no processor on a late registration, so after every restart those processors silently did not exist, and on the owed-erase path a drive's deletion went unpaid. Now they make their processors and backfill from their persisted cursor, or per `startFrom` if they have none.

## The exception
A purged drive's header is erased with it: its stream is a lone `PURGE_DOCUMENT` marker, so the factory receives a minimal header with empty `slug` and `name`. A factory that selects by slug or name then makes no processor for that drive, its deletion stays owed, and the manager logs a warning. Selecting drives by id avoids the trap, which is one more reason for "Processors need full drive IDs when drive slugs are not unique."

{"title":"A replayed operation carries the document's latest state by default, which can be newer than the operation; replayState chooses collapse, exact or no state instead","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T19:51:45.908Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T19:51:45.908Z","description":"Replays (first install, restart catch-up, rerun, retry) read the operation index, which keeps no resultingState; only a live delivery carries the executor's state after the operation."}

{"content":"## The claim
`context.resultingState` means different things on live and replayed deliveries. A **live** delivery always carries the executor's state after the operation. A **replay** — first install, catch-up after a restart, a rerun, a retry — reads operations from the operation index, which keeps no `resultingState`, so the manager fills it according to the record's `replayState`:

| `replayState` | A replayed operation carries |
| --- | --- |
| `latest` (default) | Every operation, with the document's latest state. It can be newer than the operation, never older than a state already delivered for that stream. |
| `collapse` | Per document stream, one delivery with the latest state; the operations it includes are skipped. Only for processors whose output depends on the latest state alone. |
| `exact` | Every operation, with its state at its own revision. Slower. |
| `operations` | Every operation, without state. |

## Consequences
- A processor that records per-operation history from `resultingState` (status at the time of each change, an audit trail, analytics on state transitions) gets the wrong answer on replay under the default: every replayed operation shows today's state. It needs `exact`, or must derive what it records from `operation.action` itself.
- Rails the code keeps: a stream whose snapshot is behind the page gets its exact state instead, so a replay never delivers a state older than its operation; a deleted document's operations pass as read, without state; in `exact`, an operation whose state cannot be rebuilt passes without state and is recorded with the error.
- Code must tolerate a missing `resultingState` anyway (the `operations` mode, deletion markers).

## Where it sits
"Read models and sync depend on resultingState and a global ordinal in OperationContext…" explains why the index's missing state matters; `replayState` is the processor-side answer to it.

{"title":"Each processor has its own delivery queue and receives one onOperations call at a time, so a slow processor delays only itself","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T19:51:51.156Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T19:51:51.156Z","description":"Batches that queue behind a running call are merged into the next one (up to 500 operations) in arrival order; backfill runs on the same queue, and registerFactory returns before it finishes."}

{"content":"## The claim
The processor manager does not call processors from the projection pipeline directly: it puts each matching batch on the processor's own queue. A queue runs one task at a time, so a processor receives one `onOperations` call at a time, and the next begins after the previous resolves. Consecutive live batches waiting behind a running call go out together as a single call, in the order they arrived, capped at 500 operations (the operation index's page size), so a busy processor pays once per drain rather than once per document batch. A slow processor delays only its own queue; other processors and other documents keep moving.

## Consequences
- A processor's own state is touched by one call at a time; it needs no lock against itself.
- A call can be bigger than one document's batch and span documents; keep per-call work proportional to its size.
- Backfill runs on the same queue. Live batches for a backfilling processor wait behind it and skip what it already delivered. `registerFactory` resolves once the factory has run and its processors are bound, before their backfills finish: to wait, watch `lastOrdinal` through `get()` or `getAll()`.
- A failed merged call holds the cursor below its lowest ordinal (see "A throwing processor is isolated and never retried automatically…").
- Waiting inside a call for your own write's `READ_READY` blocks this very queue ("Waiting for a write to reach READ_READY from inside a processor is an anti-pattern…").

{"title":"Processor delivery is at-least-once, except that a crash between two concurrently projected documents can leave the lower ordinals unreplayed","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T19:51:58.349Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T19:51:58.349Z","description":"Restarts, retries and a backfill reading an operation whose live batch is still in flight all repeat operations, so writes must be idempotent; the crash window is the one documented loss."}

{"content":"## The claim
A processor may be handed the same operation more than once:
- after a restart, catch-up replays from the persisted cursor;
- after `tracked.retry()`, the processor replays from its cursor;
- when a backfill reads an operation whose live batch is still on its way to the manager: another document's pass has already raised the high-water mark past it, so the live batch delivers it again when it lands.

So delivery is at-least-once, not exactly-once. The processor migration guide's line that "each operation is delivered exactly once — there is no replay" is wrong at this version.

The documented exception runs the other way. Documents are projected concurrently and a processor's cursor is raised to a batch's maximum ordinal when that is higher. If the reactor crashes after the higher ordinal's cursor was persisted, but before a concurrently projected document's lower ordinals were delivered, catch-up starts above them and they are never replayed.

## What to do
- Make every write idempotent: upsert rows keyed by document id and operation index, and put dedup keys in documents you dispatch to.
- Derive counts (count rows keyed by document and index) instead of incrementing counters per delivery.
- A processor that must be complete needs a way to rebuild. The reactor has one: `IProcessor.clear()` with `clearScope` lets a processor be cleared and replayed from its first ordinal (code at e0f277d). The docs describe no automatic sweep for the crash gap, so scheduling such rebuilds is an operator decision, not a guarantee.

{"content":"## The claim
A deleted drive's cursor rows are kept until each of its processors has received the deletion. A processor that was not running when the drive was deleted (its factory was not registered yet after a restart, or was being reloaded), or whose `onOperations` threw on it, still receives it: the next time its factory is registered, the factory is called for the deleted drive, and that processor receives only the drive's `DELETE_DOCUMENT` (or its `PURGE_DOCUMENT` if the drive has been purged since), then `onDisconnect`. Only then do its rows go.

## Details that decide behaviour
- Neither `registerFactory` nor a later registration or unregistration under the same identifier waits for that delivery, so a processor that hangs on it holds up no reload. A re-registration delivers the deletion again only if the delivery in flight settles with the drive still owed.
- An errored processor receives its drive's deletion too. One that throws on it stays in `getAll()` as errored, and its `retry()` calls the factory for the drive and delivers the deletion again.
- Unregistering keeps a factory's cursor rows as *released*: a re-registration starts every processor afresh per `startFrom`, but still owes the deletion of a drive deleted in between.
- A factory registered for the first time after a drive's deletion never had processors for it and is not called for it.
- **The trap:** a purged drive's header is minimal (only `id` and `documentType`), so a factory that selects drives by `slug` or `name` makes no processor for it, the deletion stays owed, and the manager logs a warning. Only the rows of processors that received the deletion are removed.

## Why it is built this way
Before 731112ce06 the deletion pass deleted every cursor row of the drive at once, so a factory registered after a restart, or an errored processor, lost the deletion for good and its namespace kept the drive's rows. 34e14393cb closed the reload gap: reactor-api unregisters and re-registers every package on each package change, and a drive deleted inside that window used to leave no row behind.

## Evidence
Academy › Reference › Reactor › Processors, § "Deletion and erasure" (last bullet). Commits 731112ce06 "keep a deleted drive's cursor rows until each processor has its deletion", 34e14393cb "release a factory's cursor rows on unregister", fd411760a9 "list processors that threw on their drive's deletion", 7d64621f1d and 88017fc40a (registration does not wait on owed deletions).","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T19:52:16.741Z"}

{"content":"## The mental model: a lens, not a store of record

A document's operation log is authoritative but not always convenient. Asking "which todos did Alice complete last week?" should not mean replaying an entire log on every request. That is what processors are for: event-driven handlers that subscribe to the operation stream and maintain a **read model** on the side.

Think of each processor as a materialised view. It:

1. Subscribes to one or more document types (or specific documents).
2. Receives every matching operation after it is appended: at least once, and in order only within one document's scope and branch.
3. Updates its own storage — a table, an index, a counter.

Reducers stay lean; queries stay fast; neither side has to know about the other.

## Why replayability is the important property

A processor's only input is an append-only log it does not own. That makes its output *derived data*, and derived data is disposable. Add a counter, fix an aggregation bug, reshape the output — then drop the processor's state and replay from operation zero. The log never changed; only the lens did.

This is what makes processors forgiving in a way that a schema migration on a mutable table is not. A bad migration destroys information. A bad processor produces a wrong view over information that is still fully intact upstream, so the fix is mechanical rather than archaeological.

Two conditions keep a rebuild honest at v6.2.3-dev.91+e0f277d. Delivery is at-least-once, so the replayed view must come out the same when an operation arrives twice: idempotent writes, not increments. And a replayed operation carries the document's *latest* state by default (`replayState: "latest"`), so a view built from `context.resultingState` rebuilds every operation against today's state; a history-shaped view needs `replayState: "exact"` or must derive from `operation.action`.

## Where the line falls

The division of labour is sharp:

- **Reducer** — "what is this document now?" Validation, state transitions. Must be pure.
- **Processor** — "what else should happen because of that operation?" Aggregates, indexes, notifications, side effects.

Counting completed todos across all history belongs in a processor: doing it in the reducer couples the document's state size to its age. Sending mail on assignment belongs in a processor too, because reducers cannot perform I/O. Rejecting an empty title belongs in the reducer, because that check must run *before* the action becomes an operation.

_Source: apps/academy/docs/academy/02-Learn/06-switchboard/03-processors-and-read-models.mdx (Powerhouse v6.2.2-dev.45)._

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T19:59:47.042Z","description":"Generated with ph generate processor --type relationalDb: migrations for the schema, one namespace per drive, a document_id column and a document-scope filter so a deleted document's rows can go."}

{"content":"Generate with `ph generate processor --name <name> --type relationalDb --document-types <type>`. It creates a processor class (extends `RelationalDbProcessor<DB>`), `migrations.ts` (up/down functions with a Kysely-style schema builder), `factory.ts` (opens a namespaced DB per drive) and `schema.ts` (TypeScript types generated from the migration with `ph generate migration-file --path <migrations-file>`).

**Lifecycle.**
- `initAndUpgrade()` runs the processor's migrations on startup.
- `onOperations()` handles each batch. That includes erasure: on `DELETE_DOCUMENT` or `PURGE_DOCUMENT` the processor deletes the document's rows, or drops its namespace when the deleted document is its own drive (`deleteDocumentRows`, `isNamespaceDrive`, `dropNamespace`).
- `onDisconnect()` cleans up resources; it also runs when the factory is unregistered or reloaded, so it is never where rows are erased.

**What erasure needs from the schema and factory.**
- Every table records the document a row came from in a `document_id` (or `documentId`) column. The tutorial's `todo` table gained `document_id varchar(255) not null`.
- The filter's `scope` includes `"document"` alongside `"global"`, because the deletion operations live in the document scope.
- The factory constructs the processor with `driveHeader.id` as a fourth argument, which `isNamespaceDrive` compares against.

Namespaces (`getNamespace(driveId)`) prevent data collisions between drives. Data is exposed through subgraphs with `TodoIndexerProcessor.query(driveId, relationalDb)`, a type-safe query builder on that namespace; the resolver needs only `subgraph.relationalDb`, not the reactor client.

Checked against `packages/codegen/src/templates/processors/relational-db/processor.ts` and `factory.ts` at e0f277d.

{"title":"context.resultingState is the whole document serialized with each scope and the header at its top level, so the global state is JSON.parse(resultingState).global","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:00:06.706Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:00:06.706Z","description":"Unlike a reducer's scoped state argument, a processor gets { header, global, local, ... } as one JSON string; the header is written last so a scope named header cannot shadow it."}

{"content":"## The claim
A processor's `context.resultingState` is a JSON **string** of the whole document after the operation: every scope's state as a top-level key, plus the header. To read the global state, parse it and take `.global`:

```ts
const state = JSON.parse(context.resultingState);
const global = state.global;   // the global scope's state
const header = state.header;   // id, documentType, revision, ...
```

The executor builds it as `JSON.stringify({ ...document.state, header: document.header })`, header last, so that a state key named `header` cannot replace the real header (`packages/reactor/src/executor/document-action-handler.ts` at e0f277d).

## Why it is worth knowing
It is easy to assume `resultingState` is the state of the operation's own scope, because that is what a reducer receives ("The state argument a reducer receives is already the scoped state"). Reading `JSON.parse(resultingState).items` when the items live under `.global.items` silently yields `undefined`.

## Conditions
- This is the shape of a **live** delivery. On a replay, what `resultingState` holds depends on the record's `replayState` (latest by default, exact, or none): "A replayed operation carries the document's latest state by default…".
- It can be absent: the `operations` replay mode, and deletion markers. Handle `DELETE_DOCUMENT` / `PURGE_DOCUMENT` before parsing.
- It is a string, so each parse costs a full deserialization of the document; parse once per operation you actually need.

## Evidence

{"content":"## The finding

The document view (`DocumentSnapshot`, `SlugMapping`) is a read model, but it lives in the **reactor store**. It is committed inside the purge fence transaction, on the same single PGlite lane as the operation log. A document read was two queries on that lane: the snapshot, then `MAX(index)` per scope on `Operation`. Both queued behind every executor transaction, view-indexing chunk, sync load and `VACUUM`.

The ADR measured the cost on Sektar's store (18 GB, 13,198 transactions) under 9 writes per second:

| Read | Idle p95 | Under 9 writes/s |
| --- | --- | --- |
| document read on the write lane | 46 ms | 115–206 ms |
| typed listing on the write lane | 91 ms | 426–537 ms |
| index-backed read on the read store | 36–53 ms | 36–53 ms |

## The coupling ran both ways

Reads depended on the write store for identity, and writes depended on the read store. Every mutation read the view: target resolution (`resolveWriteTarget` on `SlugMapping` and `DocumentSnapshot`), the drive client's node checks (the whole drive document), the model subgraph's type check, cascade discovery, and a read-back after `waitForJob`, twice. Every authorized GraphQL field also resolved its identifier through the view and checked permission tables that lived on the read-model store.

## So what

The degradation is structural, not a tuning problem, because the reads and writes share one queue. That is the case for "The reactor client is split into a read half ...", "Mutations resolve their targets from a write-side WriteIdentity table ..." and "Permission tables live in the reactor store behind a per-process cache ...". The ADR also notes that the full fix, moving the document view to the read store, is a later decision.

## Evidence

{"title":"In-process read-after-write stays job-based: READ_READY is set only after the pre-ready read models commit, so any read model an in-process reader relies on must be registered pre-ready or it silently breaks execute-then-read","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:02:31.942Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:02:31.942Z","description":"On one store, 'execute, then read' needs no token. Remote clients bound a read after their own write with the consistency argument on document, findDocuments and relationship queries."}

{"content":"## The decision

The job lifecycle reaches `READ_READY` only after the **pre-ready** read models have committed the write. So in-process, "execute, then read" keeps its guarantee on one store without any token. The read half sees the write once the job is `READ_READY`, which is what a `WriteHandle`'s `readable` stage waits for.

The guarantee holds only for read models registered pre-ready (see "Custom read models registered via withReadModel run in pre-ready phase ..."). The ADR states the consequence for the next step: when the document view is duplicated into the read store, that copy **must be registered pre-ready**. Registered post-ready, it would silently break every in-process reader, because `READ_READY` would fire before the copy held the write.

## Remote clients

A remote client cannot observe the local job. The GraphQL `document`, `findDocuments` and relationship queries therefore accept an optional `consistency` token argument, and a client passes the token from its own write's receipt to bound the read (see "Consistency tokens in the reactor guarantee read-after-write correctness ..."). Mutation resolvers read back once with `readAsCaller(read, receipt, subject, branch)`, which is `read.get` with the receipt's token. The ADR expects the token to become the only read-after-write path for remote clients once the view moves to the read store.

## Evidence

`docs/adr/0006-reactor-client-halves.md`, Decision 6 "Read-after-write stays job-based", Decision 3 (the `consistency` argument, `readAsCaller`), and Confidence and revisit.

{"title":"KnexAnalyticsStore now writes and reads its naive timestamp columns as UTC, so series rows written earlier on a non-UTC host read back shifted by that host's offset and need a one-time manual UPDATE","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:06:10.608Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:06:10.608Z","description":"Binding a JS Date made node-postgres store host-local wall clock. UTC hosts are unaffected; others must shift old rows by their known historical offset, which is deliberately not automated."}

{"content":"## The failure

`KnexAnalyticsStore` stores a series' `start` and `end` in **naive** `timestamp` columns (no time zone). Earlier versions bound JS `Date` values, and node-postgres serializes a `Date` into such a column as the **host's local wall clock**, then parses reads back as host-local. On one host that was self-consistent. But the stored values depended on the writing host's timezone, and they disagreed with `BrowserAnalyticsStore`, which uses UTC.

The store now renders every `DateTime` crossing into SQL as an explicit UTC ISO string and reads the columns back as UTC, so both stores agree on the same logical data whatever the host timezone.

## Consequence for existing data

- A deployment that always ran on **UTC hosts**, the common server case, stored UTC wall clock all along and is unaffected.
- Rows written on a **non-UTC host** are stored shifted by that host's offset and now read back shifted. A row written at 10:00 UTC on a UTC+2 host was stored as 12:00 and now reads as 12:00 UTC. Time-bucketed analytics put such rows in the wrong period, silently.

## The repair

A one-time `UPDATE` shifting the affected rows by the known historical offset:

```sql
UPDATE "AnalyticsSeries"
SET "start" = "start" - interval '2 hours',
    "end"   = "end"   - interval '2 hours';
```

It is **deliberately not automated**. Only the operator knows the historical offset, whether it varied with daylight saving, and whether rows came from several hosts.

## Where it sits in the vault

It is the failure "The Analytics Engine uses luxon DateTime everywhere because a JS Date cannot report whether it was constructed in UTC" was designed to prevent. The engine used luxon on its API, but the store's SQL binding still passed a JS `Date`, and the timezone mistake happened at that last boundary.

## Evidence

`packages/analytics-engine/knex/MIGRATION.md`, whole page. Code at e0f277d: `packages/analytics-engine/knex/src/KnexAnalyticsStore.ts` (class comment "Every DateTime crossing into SQL is rendered as an explicit UTC ISO string (never bound as a JS Date ...)"; `_toUtcIso`); fix commit `a4d6c4b9b9` "fix(analytics): anchor periods and timestamps to UTC (#3175)".

{"title":"Operation-index ordinals come from a Postgres serial, so a rolled-back commit leaves a permanent hole and, when several executors commit at once, a hole can be transient, so a read model can neither demand contiguous ordinals nor simply skip a gap","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:28:20.993Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:28:20.993Z","description":"Demanding contiguity stalled the attachment reference read model at the first hole; skipping blindly drops the late row under REACTOR_WORKERS. The reactor now asks which transactions are open."}

{"content":"## The mechanism

`operation_index_operations.ordinal` is a Postgres `serial` (migration 009). The value is drawn inside `executeCommit`'s transaction, and several statements run after the insert (memberships, removals, group references), any of which can throw. On rollback the sequence value stays consumed. **A hole is normal**, and when commits are serialised it is permanent: no row will ever take it.

Commits are serialised by default (one executor, `maxConcurrency ?? 1`). With **`REACTOR_WORKERS`** the reactor starts one executor per worker (`executorStartCount = pool.numWorkers`), and two commit transactions can overlap. Then a hole can be **transient**: ordinal 5 is taken by a transaction still open while 6 has already committed. A reader that sees 6 and not 5 cannot tell the two cases apart from the ordinals alone.

## Why both naive policies fail

- **Demand contiguity.** The attachment reference read model refused to advance past a missing ordinal ("cannot advance past missing ordinal 12"), re-threw on every later write, and crashed Switchboard at boot. It did not even index the contiguous rows before the hole.
- **Skip the gap.** Advancing past a hole is correct only if the hole is permanent. Under concurrent commits, the late row 5 would arrive below the cursor and be filtered out for good.

## The resolution at e0f277d

`BaseReadModel` tracks a `ContiguousCursor` and a `SettledWatermark` (`packages/reactor/src/read-models/base-read-model.ts`). The watermark "knows when an ordinal gap is final by asking which transactions are open" (`packages/reactor/src/catch-up/settled-watermark.ts`): it probes the sequence head and the open transaction ids, and treats a gap as settled only once every transaction that could still fill it has ended. This is the general answer the investigation's options lacked. Its recommended fix (advance past holes) carried exactly the residual risk named above.

## Evidence

`docs/upstream-bugs-6.2.2-dev.85-investigation.md`, Bug 6 (a) (serial sequence, statements after the insert, repro cases 1–3, the discarded contiguous row) and (d) Option B's residual risk under REACTOR_WORKERS. Code at e0f277d: `packages/reactor/src/storage/migrations/009_create_operation_index_tables.ts` (`addColumn("ordinal", "serial", …)`), `packages/reactor/src/core/reactor-builder.ts` (`executorStartCount = pool.numWorkers`), `packages/reactor/src/catch-up/settled-watermark.ts`.
","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:28:20.993Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:28:28.540Z","description":"Before, ReactorBuilder awaited each read-model factory unguarded, so a failure that is non-fatal at run time (logged, other models carry on) became 'App crashed' at startup."}

{"content":"## The decision

`ReactorBuilder` registers read-model factories and awaits each one while building the module. The investigation found that loop **unguarded**, two lines below a `processorManager.init()` that **was** wrapped in try/catch. A read model whose catch-up threw at boot, such as the attachment reference model stalled on an ordinal hole, propagated straight to Switchboard's `logger.error("App crashed: @error", e)`. The same failure at run time was only logged while the other models carried on.

At e0f277d the loop is guarded like the processor manager. Each factory runs in a try/catch, and a failure calls `startDegraded(...)` naming the read model by registration order plus the factory's function name when it has one ("A read model that cannot build or catch up must not take the reactor down with it: log and start degraded, as the indexers above do").

## Why it matters

One broken projection no longer takes a whole Switchboard offline. The trade-off is visibility: a degraded start is a log line, not an outage, so a missing read model shows up as wrong or empty reads (see "Read models on another database handle are not fenced against a purge ..." for another read-model failure that is equally quiet).

{"title":"A processor that keeps its read model in memory is silently partial after a restart, because its persisted cursor resumes delivery after the operations that built it","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:29:18.482Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:29:18.482Z","description":"Its ProcessorCursor row survives a reboot and outranks startFrom, so an in-memory counter restarts at zero but is fed only the gap. Persist the view, or clear() and rerun."}

{"content":"## The claim

A processor whose read model lives only in the processor object (a class field, a `Map`, a counter) gives wrong answers after the host restarts. It does not start again from zero and rebuild. It starts from its persisted cursor, so the view in memory starts empty and only receives the operations that arrive after the restart.

## The mechanism

The processor manager persists one cursor row per processor in the reactor's `ProcessorCursor` table. On startup it loads every row (`loadAllCursors` in `packages/reactor/src/processors/processor-manager.ts`). When it binds a processor, a cached row that is not released wins: the processor's `lastOrdinal` is set from the row, and `startFrom` is consulted only when no such row exists (see "startFrom applies only when no cursor row positions a processor: a restart keeps the persisted cursor, while unregistering releases it"). Catch-up then replays only the gap above that ordinal.

The cursor moves after each delivery succeeds, even if the processor's own state was never written anywhere durable. After a restart the cursor remembers how far the processor got, but the processor has forgotten what it built.

## Evidence

The Learn lesson "Processors and read models" presents a minimal `TodoStatsProcessor` that keeps `private counts = { added: 0, completed: 0, removed: 0 }`, increments it in `onOperations`, exposes it through `getStats()`, and closes with "That's it." On a Switchboard that has been restarted once, `getStats()` returns only the operations since the restart, and nothing says so. The same lesson says the view can be rebuilt by replaying from operation zero, but a restart does not do that.

## Conditions

- It applies on any host whose reactor store survives the process. Switchboard with PGlite on disk or with Postgres is one (checked in the manager code). A host with a throwaway in-memory store gets fresh cursors on every boot and so happens to rebuild from zero.
- A package reload behaves differently. reactor-api unregisters and re-registers every package on change, which releases the cursor rows, so the next registration starts per `startFrom` (default `"beginning"`) and rebuilds from history.
- Increments are wrong for a second, independent reason. Delivery is at-least-once, so a redelivered batch counts twice (see "Processor delivery is at-least-once, except that a crash between two concurrently projected documents can leave the lower ordinals unreplayed").

## What to do instead

Put the view where the cursor is, in storage that persists with the reactor: the processor host module's `relationalDb` (or an analytics store), with idempotent writes keyed by document and operation. If a view really must stay in memory, give the processor `clear()` and trigger a rebuild with the manager's `rerun({ clear: true })` after boot. This lets you predict when a dashboard built on such a processor goes quietly wrong: the first restart after deploy, not the first bug.

Checked against `packages/reactor/src/processors/processor-manager.ts` (`loadAllCursors`, cursor binding) and `packages/shared/processors/types.ts` (`IProcessor.clear`, `ProcessorRerunOptions`) at e0f277d.

{"title":"A switchboard paces processor catch-up against request load: PH_CATCH_UP_PRIORITY=dynamic, the default, moves between levels 1 and 6 by request p95 latency and event-loop delay, while 0 stops catch-up and 7 runs it flat out","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:41:04.086Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:41:04.086Z","description":"Each level sets backfill slots, page size and how pages give way; level 4 is the old behaviour. The controller drops above 250 ms p95 or 100 ms loop delay and stays at 5 or below while busy."}

{"content":"## The mechanism

When processors catch up (a fresh read model, a restart behind the log, a backfill), their reads compete with user requests for the store and the event loop. Since `278d0ec3cd` a switchboard builds its reactor with a **catch-up priority** (`packages/reactor/src/processors/catch-up-priority.ts` at e0f277d). Each level is a fixed recipe:

| Level | Backfill slots | Ordinals per page | Between pages |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | 0 | stop: requests only |
| 1–3 | 1–2 | 100–250 | pause 50–10 ms |
| 4 | 3 | 500 | yield (the behaviour before priorities existed) |
| 5–6 | 4–6 | 500–1000 | yield |
| 7 | 8 | 2000 | none: catch-up only |

`PH_CATCH_UP_PRIORITY` is `dynamic` (the default) or a fixed level from `0` to `7`. Anything else warns and runs dynamic.

## The dynamic controller

Every second it samples a 5 s window: requests completed and their p95 latency, the main thread's p99 event-loop delay, and the time since the last request. It **drops** a level when p95 exceeds 250 ms or loop delay exceeds 100 ms, counts a tick as calm below 125 ms and 50 ms, climbs no higher than 5 while requests are active, and stays within 1–6. Catch-up always progresses and requests always get a turn. It starts at 4. The current level and its reason appear in `ph vetra` and `ph switchboard`'s catch-up line ("priority 4 dynamic").

## Conditions

- It paces only catch-up, the backfill reads. Live operations still reach processors as they arrive.
- The load signal is the HTTP server's own request recorder plus loop delay. Load the switchboard cannot see (another process on the same database) does not move it.
- Keyframe clean-up paces itself by the same priority (see "Keyframe clean-up needs no lock against writers…").

## In the vault

This is the shipped form of the idea in "A load-aware priority controller can yield background read-model work to user requests.", a demo note that described an eight-level system still to be tested. The eight levels are 0–7 here. Whether responsiveness holds under all loads is still not established by the source, only the controller's rules.

## What it lets you do

Leave a production switchboard on `dynamic`. Pin `7` for a maintenance window where catch-up should finish as fast as possible, and `0` to freeze catch-up while you investigate a slow processor.

{"title":"Processor timing measures the wall-clock time a processor's queue awaited, not CPU, so one processor's busy time never exceeds the window while the sum over processors can, and its read time includes waiting for the store connection","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:41:11.165Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:41:11.165Z","description":"basic (default) times each processor; detailed adds document types and slow-batch warnings. High read time under concurrent backfills means waiting on the store; throttling is not busy time."}

{"content":"## How to read the numbers

Processor timing (`PH_PROCESSOR_TIMING`, default `basic` on a switchboard since `f196cf8eb2`) reports, per processor over a rolling window (`PH_PROCESSOR_TIMING_WINDOW_MS`, 60 s), how long its queue spent **awaiting** work, split into handler, read and fill. The Docker deployment guide (§ Telemetry, at e0f277d) spells out what that means:

- **Wall clock, not CPU.** A processor that awaits a slow database is "busy" for the whole wait.
- **Per processor ≤ window, sum unbounded.** One processor's busy time cannot exceed the window, but processors run at once, so the sum across processors can. Busy times are not shares of one CPU.
- **Read includes waiting for the store connection.** "Under concurrent backfills, a high read time means 'waited on the store', not 'this query is slow'."
- **Throttling is not work.** Waiting for a backfill slot and pausing between pages are the catch-up priority throttling the processor (see "A switchboard paces processor catch-up against request load…"), and they count toward no busy time.

The same breakdown appears in the console. `ph vetra` and `ph switchboard` print `catch-up slowest (60 s): FilesIndex·files 41s (handler 12s read 25s fill 4.1s) 3.1k op/s eta 59s` and a summary when catch-up ends (`clis/ph-cli/README.md` § Catch-up and telemetry output). In that example the processor spent more of its time reading than handling, and under concurrent backfills that points at store contention before it points at the processor's code.

## Levels and surfaces

`basic` times each processor. `detailed` also splits by document type and logs a warning for each `onOperations` call over `PH_PROCESSOR_SLOW_BATCH_MS` (1000 ms). `off` records nothing, and `PH_TELEMETRY=off` turns processor and memory telemetry off whatever their own settings say. On a host without the `ph` console, `PH_PROCESSOR_TIMING_LOG_MS` above 0 logs the slowest processors periodically while catching up. Everything lands in one surface: the `processorTiming` inspection field, the reactor monitor's Processors tab, and the console lines.

## Why it matters

Each processor has its own queue and receives one `onOperations` call at a time ("Each processor has its own delivery queue and receives one onOperations call at a time…"), so the per-processor number is the right unit. Summing it, or reading "read" as query cost, leads to optimising the wrong thing.

## What it lets you do

Find the processor that holds catch-up back, and tell a slow handler (high handler time) from a contended store (high read time while several backfills run).

{"title":"A relational processor's per-drive namespace is not drive-scoped: every drive's instance receives each operation its filter matches from every drive, so each namespace holds rows for all drives' documents","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:43:04.000Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:43:04.000Z","description":"The processor manager delivers by filter alone, with no drive-membership check, so a query by driveId returns everything. Scope rows to one drive by intersecting with that drive's file nodes."}

{"content":"A relational processor's factory runs once per drive and opens a namespace per drive (`<ClassName>_<driveId>`, dashes to underscores). That reads like data isolation; it is storage separation only.

**Mechanism.** In `packages/reactor/src/processors/processor-manager.ts` at e0f277d, live delivery loops over every bound processor and passes it `items.filter((op) => matchesFilter(op, tracked.record.filter))`. The tracked processor's `driveId` is consulted only to deliver that drive's own deletion. The scaffold filter is `documentId: ["*"]` with the model's `documentType`, so every drive's instance receives every matching document's operations, whichever drive the document is in.

**Consequences.**
- With N drives, each namespace holds a row set for all drives' documents; storage grows with drives × documents.
- `MyProcessor.query(driveId, db)` returns all of them: a query by `driveId` alone does not scope to that drive.
- To scope rows, the subgraphs reference reads the drive (`ctx.clients.read.get(driveId)`, typed `DocumentDriveDocument`) and keeps rows whose `document_id` is a file node in `state.global.nodes`. And because the query builder checks no document permissions, `assertCanRead(driveId, ctx)` comes first when the data is not public.
- Overriding the static `getNamespace(driveId)` to share one namespace removes the duplication, but then the scaffold's deletion branch — `dropNamespace()` when the deleted document is the drive — must change, or one drive's deletion drops every drive's data.

This qualifies "RelationalDbProcessor provides a type-safe base class with per-drive namespace isolation": the namespaces are isolated from each other, their contents are not limited to their drive. Analytics processors share one store and scope by series source instead.
","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:43:04.000Z"}

{"title":"After the first scaffold a processor's files, not its Vetra document, decide what codegen registers: it never rewrites them, never unregisters an app, and reads apps, type and document types back from the files","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:43:12.000Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:43:12.000Z","description":"So ADD_DOCUMENT_TYPE leaves the filter alone, REMOVE_PROCESSOR_APP does not unregister, a rename scaffolds a second folder and the type is fixed. Edit the files, then keep the document in step."}

{"content":"The processor document drives the first scaffold only. Per the processors-subgraphs skill (972f193395), every file under `processors/<id>/` is written once, when missing — `processor.ts`, `factory.ts`, and for relational processors `migrations.ts` and `schema.ts` are yours; `index.ts` re-exports `factory.js` and `processor.js`. In `processors/connect.ts` and `processors/switchboard.ts` codegen adds an import and a `processorFactoryBuilders` entry for each app the processor runs in and never removes one.

When `ph migrate` or `ph generate all` regenerate a processor folder they reconstruct the processor from its files, not from the document: the apps from which of `connect.ts` and `switchboard.ts` register it, the type from what `processor.ts` imports (`RelationalDbProcessor` or `IAnalyticsStore` — the import sniffing whose failure mode is "Processor type is detected by sniffing imports, so a relational processor is misclassified as analytics after a migration writes an analytics stub"), and the document types from the `documentType` string-literal array in `factory.ts`. A folder with files but no `processor.ts`, which no file imports as `./processor`, counts as hand-written and is left alone with its registrations; a folder without a processor's shape at all (shared helpers) is left alone with a warning.

What document changes still do after the scaffold:
- `ADD_DOCUMENT_TYPE` / `REMOVE_DOCUMENT_TYPE`: nothing to the code — edit the `filter` in `factory.ts`.
- `ADD_PROCESSOR_APP`: registers in the new app's file. `REMOVE_PROCESSOR_APP`: does not unregister — delete the import and array entry by hand.
- A new name scaffolds a second folder beside the first; delete the old folder and its entries.
- The type cannot change in place: delete the folder and entries, then `SET_PROCESSOR_TYPE` (any action on a confirmed document reruns codegen).

So the files are the truth, and keeping the document in step is a discipline, not something codegen enforces — the Vetra drive should still describe what the package ships, because agents read it. `ph generate processor --dir <id>` repairs one existing folder the same way: missing files, registration, missing dependencies.
","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:43:12.000Z"}

{"title":"A relational processor can be unit-tested with @powerhousedao/shared/processors/testing: createTestRelationalDb for an in-memory PGlite, runProcessorMigrations for the namespace, and operationsWithContext or testOperation to feed onOperations, which codegen's starter processor.test.ts already does","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:43:42.000Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:43:42.000Z","description":"No reactor or drive is booted. Neither helper sets context.resultingState, so a processor that reads state from it sees nothing in a test until the test adds it."}

{"content":"The repo now ships what "A processor's indexing logic can be tested against an in-memory database without booting the reactor" describes: `packages/shared/processors/testing.ts`, exported as `@powerhousedao/shared/processors/testing`.

- `createTestRelationalDb()` returns an `IRelationalDb` on an in-memory PGlite.
- `runProcessorMigrations(db, namespace, up)` opens the namespace as a factory does and runs the migration's `up` in it.
- `operationsWithContext(document, scopes?)` turns a document built with the model's own reducer and creators into the `OperationWithContext[]` `onOperations` receives: sorted by timestamp, branch `main`, ordinals 1..n.
- `testOperation({ documentId, documentType, type, input?, scope?, index?, timestampUtcMs? })` builds one operation without a reducer — the starter test uses it for `CREATE_DOCUMENT` and `DELETE_DOCUMENT`.

Every new relational processor gets a starter `processor.test.ts` on these helpers (template `packages/codegen/src/templates/processors/relational-db/processor-test.ts`): one test writes a row for a created document, one checks that a deleted document's rows go. Adapt it whenever the migration changes. It runs under `npm run test`, not under the reducer coverage gate.

**The gap to know.** Neither helper sets `context.resultingState`. A live delivery carries it, and a processor that derives rows from state — like the processors reference's example, which skips any operation without it — receives nothing to write in a test until the test spreads its own `resultingState: JSON.stringify({ global: … })` into the context. A test that passes because the processor wrote nothing is the failure this hides.

What the helpers do not model either: delivery semantics — at-least-once repeats, ordering only within a document, the drive's deletion delivered whatever the filter, replay states. Feed a repeated operation and a `DELETE_DOCUMENT` to check idempotence and erasure.

Checked against `testing.ts` and the template at e0f277d.

{"title":"A package's own HTTP routes are served under /api/<its npm name>/ through one IHttpScope per package, shared by its subgraphs as this.http and its processors as module.http","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:43:52.308Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:43:52.308Z","description":"The npm-name prefix makes route collisions between packages impossible; asking for the scope twice returns the same one, and a duplicate method+path on a scope throws."}

{"content":"## The claim

A reactor package can serve plain HTTP endpoints of its own beside the GraphQL API. It registers them in code against an **HTTP scope** the host hands it, and every route lands under the package's npm name:

```
https://switchboard.example/api/@powerhousedao/reports/reports/42
                           └──┘ └──────────────────────┘ └───────┘
                          prefix      package name       your path
```

There is one `IHttpScope` per package. A subgraph reads it off itself as `this.http` (in `onSetup`); a processor takes it in its constructor as `module.http` from its factory — **optional** there, because a processor also runs in the browser, where there is no HTTP server. Both are the same object: asking twice returns the same scope, so a hot reload cannot accumulate namespaces, and registering the same method and path twice on one scope throws.

## Why namespace by npm name

Packages are loaded into one host by people who never coordinate. Prefixing every path with the package's own registry name makes a collision between two packages impossible by construction, and makes a URL say which package answers it. This vault's own REST surface is an instance: `https://switchboard.knowledge-vault.vetra.io/api/@powerhousedao/knowledge-note/...` is the `@powerhousedao/knowledge-note` package's scope.

## Conditions

- Paths are relative to the namespace: absolute paths, `..` segments and URL-shaped paths throw, so a package cannot name a path outside it.
- Provider webhooks are a different surface: flat `/webhooks/<token>` URLs with no package in the path ("A package webhook URL is a flat /webhooks/<token>…").
- The host releases the whole scope when the package unloads ("Package HTTP routes need no manual cleanup…").

## Code check

`packages/reactor-api/src/http/route-service.ts` at v6.2.3-dev.91+e0f277d: `PACKAGE_ROUTE_SEGMENT = "api"` ("The segment package routes live under, inside the host's base path"), core's own services register under `@powerhousedao/reactor-api`, and a second registration throws "Route … is already registered by …". The processor side is the optional `http?: IHttpScope` on the processor host module.

## Evidence

"Hosting HTTP routes" (opening, §§ "Subgraphs", "Processors", the paragraph after the processor example, § "What the scope does not have").
","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:43:52.308Z"}

{"title":"A package route requires a verified Renown bearer by default, yet on a host with authentication disabled a renown route serves anonymous callers, so a handler that needs an identity must check ctx.user rather than trust its auth setting","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:43:58.708Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:43:58.708Z","description":"public must be written out; renown-optional verifies a bearer if present; a custom RouteAuthorizer resolves no principal, so ctx.user stays undefined. ctx.authEnabled says if the host checks."}

{"content":"## The claim

`auth` on a package route defaults to `"renown"`: a route registered with no options requires a verifiable bearer and answers `401` without one. Public routes must be declared as such. But the default does not guarantee an identity: **on a host running with authentication disabled, every caller is anonymous and a `renown` route serves them anyway.** A handler whose decision depends on who is calling has to check `ctx.user`, and `ctx.authEnabled` tells it whether the host checked at all.

| `auth` | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `"renown"` (default) | a verifiable bearer is required; none is a `401` |
| `"renown-optional"` | a bearer is verified if present; absent, `ctx.user` is undefined instead of a `401` — for handlers that make their own per-document decision |
| `"public"` | no identity checked; `ctx.user` undefined |
| a `RouteAuthorizer` | your gate, run before the handler on the raw `IncomingMessage`, returning `{ authorized: true }`, a `{ status, message }` refusal or a whole `Response` |

## The second sharp edge

**A custom authorizer resolves no principal.** `ctx.user` is `undefined` on a route with a function `auth`, exactly as on a `public` one. If you need the caller's identity *and* a custom rule, use `renown` and apply the extra rule inside the handler.

## What the context carries

`ctx.user` has the same name and shape as a subgraph resolver's `ctx.user`; `user.appKey` is the `did:key` of the app instance that issued the token, so a route can act as the principal that signs actions. `ctx.authEnabled` is `false` on a `public` route, on a custom authorizer and on a host with authentication disabled. `ctx.transport` gives `{ proto, host, prefix, baseUrl }` resolved through any reverse proxy, instead of reading `x-forwarded-*` yourself; `ctx.signal` aborts when the client disconnects.

## Code check

`packages/reactor-api/src/http/route-service.ts` at v6.2.3-dev.91+e0f277d authenticates with `spec.auth ?? "renown"`.

## Evidence

"Hosting HTTP routes" §§ "Authentication" (table, examples, "Custom authentication", "Two sharp edges") and "The route context".
","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:43:58.708Z"}

{"field":"correctPattern","value":"Leave auth at renown (or renown-optional for per-document decisions) and gate on ctx.user / ctx.authEnabled inside the handler; for a custom rule that also needs identity, use renown plus the rule in the handler, not a RouteAuthorizer.","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:43:58.708Z"}

{"title":"The package HTTP scope has no middleware: a route's auth, body handling, prefix matching and size cap are declared on its registration, so its behaviour is readable from one place","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:44:04.883Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:44:04.883Z","description":"body is parsed, raw (exact bytes as ctx.rawBody), stream or none; routes match in registration order; nodeRoute hands raw Node req/res to protocols that must own the socket."}

{"content":"## The claim

There is no `scope.use()`. Everything that would be middleware elsewhere is a **declarative field** of the registration — `auth`, `body`, `prefix`, `maxBodyBytes` — so what a route does is readable from where it is registered. Handlers take a Fetch `Request` and the route context and return a Fetch `Response`; `get`, `post`, `put`, `patch`, `delete` and `head` are shorthands with an optional options object before the handler, and `route({ method: [...], path, ... })` puts one handler on several methods.

## Body modes

| `body` | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `"parsed"` (default) | buffered, readable through the `Request` (`await request.json()` / `text()`); the bytes go in verbatim |
| `"raw"` | buffered, and also handed over as `ctx.rawBody`, byte for byte |
| `"stream"` | not buffered; the `Request` body is the live request stream |
| `"none"` | the body is not read at all |

`"raw"` is the mode for anything that verifies a signature over the exact bytes received; the default body cap is 1 MiB.

## Matching rules

- A wildcard param joins sub-paths: `blobs/*rest` gives `ctx.params.rest = "a/b/c.txt"`.
- `prefix: true` makes a route also answer every path below it, with no param for the rest — prefer the wildcard when you need the sub-path.
- Routes within a scope match **in registration order**, so register a specific route before a prefix route that would swallow it.
- There is no `OPTIONS` registration: preflight belongs to the CORS layer, which already answers for the namespace.

## The escape hatch

`nodeRoute()` hands the handler the raw Node `IncomingMessage` and `ServerResponse`, still inside the namespace, with nothing having touched the request stream — for protocols that write to the response themselves, hijack the connection or hold a long-lived stream the Fetch shape cannot express (an MCP transport is the documented example). `auth` and `prefix` still apply; `body` and `maxBodyBytes` do not exist there, so it gives up the body cap and the uniform error handling, and the handler writes its own status codes and headers.

## Underneath

The scope sits on reactor-api's transport split: an HTTP adapter mounts `FetchHandler`s (exact match by default, prefix with `prefix: true`), and `nodeRoute` is the one path that bypasses the Fetch bridge.

## Evidence

"Hosting HTTP routes" §§ "Register a route", "Request bodies", "Serving sub-paths", "The Node escape hatch" and "What the scope does not have". Body cap: `DEFAULT_MAX_BODY_BYTES = 1_048_576` in `packages/reactor-api/src/http/route-service.ts` at v6.2.3-dev.91+e0f277d.
","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:44:04.883Z"}

{"field":"inputs","values":["get/post/put/patch/delete/head shorthands","route({ method, path, auth, body, prefix, maxBodyBytes, handler })","nodeRoute({ method, path, auth, prefix, handler })"],"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:44:04.883Z"}

{"title":"Package HTTP routes need no manual cleanup because the host releases a package's whole scope when the package is replaced, removed or the host shuts down — unlike its webhook tokens, which outlive the package","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:44:11.466Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:44:11.466Z","description":"handle.dispose() and scope.dispose() remain for routes to stop while the package stays loaded, or test scopes; disposing twice is a no-op and the path can be registered again."}

{"content":"## The claim

Packages hot-reload, so every registration is reversible — but a package does not have to reverse its own. The host releases a package's whole HTTP scope when the package is replaced or removed, and every scope when it shuts down; routes registered and forgotten are cleaned up. `handle.dispose()` and `scope.dispose()` exist for the cases the host cannot know about: a route you want to stop serving while the package stays loaded, or a scope a test stood up. Disposing something already gone is a no-op, and the same path can be registered again afterwards.

## The deliberate asymmetry

Webhook endpoints are **not** revoked when a package unloads. Their token stays valid and the endpoint answers `503` until the package returns, so a redeploy does not force re-registration with every provider ("Webhook tokens live in the reactor's relational store…"). Routes are code-shaped and ephemeral; webhook URLs are contracts with third parties.

## A processor detail

The Academy's processor example still disposes its route handle in `onDisconnect` — harmless, and useful when a processor is disconnected while its package stays loaded, but not required to avoid a stale route after a reload.

## Evidence

"Hosting HTTP routes" § "Disposal" (and the processor example's `onDisconnect`); "Receiving webhooks" § "Across restarts and reloads" ("Endpoints are not revoked on teardown").
","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:44:11.466Z"}

{"title":"A package webhook URL is a flat /webhooks/<token> whose token record carries the package and the key, so the URL leaks neither and an unknown, malformed or disarmed token all answer the same 404","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:44:16.429Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:44:16.429Z","description":"A token minted by one package can never dispatch into another's handler. A signature failure on a live token answers 401, since holding the token already proves the endpoint exists."}

{"content":"## The claim

Webhook endpoints do not live in a package's `/api/<package>/` namespace. The URL is flat and namespaceless — `/webhooks/<token>` with a 32-hex token — and the package and the logical key live in the **token record**, not the path. The URL therefore leaks neither which package receives it nor which document or account it is for, and a token minted by one package can never dispatch into another package's handler.

## Answering without revealing

The service runs its checks in a fixed order:

| Situation | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| unknown or malformed token | `404 {"error":"Unknown endpoint"}` |
| token valid, package not loaded on this host | `503` |
| `policyFor` returned `undefined` (disarmed) | `404`, byte-identical to an unknown token |
| method the policy does not allow | `405` |
| body past `maxBodyBytes` (default 1 MiB) | `413`, connection closed |
| signature verification failed | `401` |
| carries the `challengeField` value | `200 text/plain`, value echoed, handler not called |
| repeat of a seen `dedupe` value | `200`, empty, handler not called |
| anything else | whatever `onRequest` returns |

A disarmed endpoint answers exactly as one that never existed, so someone probing tokens cannot tell a live endpoint from a dead one. A verification failure answers `401` instead, because a caller holding a valid token has already proved the endpoint is there.

## Conditions

- The token is the endpoint's whole credential in the `none` scheme; a signing scheme is what makes it more than a bearer URL ("Webhook signature schemes are named by wire layout…").
- There is no rate limit in the reactor; it belongs in front, at the load balancer or CDN, where it is shared across instances. switchboard-lb pins deliveries by token for that reason and logs only an md5 of the token.

## Code check
