{"title":"Webhook tokens live in the reactor's relational store, so a key mints the same token across reloads and redeploys, any host in a fleet can serve any endpoint, and only revoke(key) retires one","updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:44:22.112Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:44:22.112Z","description":"register() once per package and name (an endpoint family), endpointFor(key) per logical key; while the owning package is unloaded its endpoints answer 503 rather than disappear."}

{"content":"## The claim

A package calls `register()` once per endpoint family (distinguished by `name` — a package receiving billing and repository events registers twice) and mints one endpoint per **logical key** with `endpointFor(key)`. The key is the package's own — a document id, an account id — and never appears in the URL. Tokens are stored in the reactor's relational store, not in the package, and `endpointFor` is idempotent per key: the same key returns the same token, so a provider already registered against a URL is not left pointing at a dead one.

## Consequences

- **Reloads and redeploys keep URLs.** A token stays valid when the package reloads, and the same key mints the same token afterwards; a redeploy does not force re-registration with every provider.
- **Absence is temporary, not fatal.** While the owning package is not loaded on a host, its endpoints answer `503` — the token is real, nothing on this host can serve it yet.
- **Fleet-friendly.** Any host in a fleet can serve any endpoint, since the token record carries the package and the key; pinning a token to one backend (as switchboard-lb does) is for warmth, not correctness.
- **Retirement is explicit.** Endpoints are not revoked on teardown; `revoke(key)` is the only thing that retires one. `list()` enumerates a family, and `endpointFor` answers with `createdAt` too.

## Conditions

`register()` rejects on a host with no webhook store, so a processor — which may also run on hosts without webhook triggers — should absorb that (`.catch(() => undefined)`) rather than fail to construct. The workflow runtime registers its own webhook endpoints through this same service, which is why workflow webhook URLs survive restarts too.

## Evidence

"Receiving webhooks" §§ "Register once, mint per key" (and the processor example's comment) and "Across restarts and reloads". Code at v6.2.3-dev.91+e0f277d: `packages/reactor-workflow/src/reactor/service.ts` holds an `IWebhookEndpoints` from the reactor's service.

{"updatedAt":"2026-11-03T20:59:02.094Z","description":"compat/test compares getMatchingSeries on one query between a local Postgres seeded from a remote dump and a PGlite loaded from dump-small.sql; CI skips compat/ and no workflow runs it at e0f277d."}

{"content":"The analytics engine ships interchangeable stores: `PostgresAnalyticsStore` on a server and `BrowserAnalyticsStore` on PGlite in the browser, and the vault's benchmark note treats the PGlite store as "a genuine alternative rather than a toy". The compatibility package (`packages/analytics-engine/compat`) is where the two are supposed to be held to the same answers. At v6.2.3-dev.91+e0f277d that check is thinner than its README suggests.

**What it tests.** `compat/test/index.test.ts` contains **one test with one query**: `getMatchingSeries` for metrics `ProtocolNetOutflow` and `PaymentsOnChain` in DAI from 2023-01-01 under the budget path `atlas/scopes/SUP/INC/TCH-001`, asserting the same number of series and deep-equal series in order. Grouping, levels of detail, other metrics and other paths are not compared.

**How it runs.** Only by hand. The Postgres side is whatever is in a local Postgres on port 5555, which a developer must start with `../pg/docker-compose.test.yml` and seed by pulling a remote database through `benchmarks/scripts/dump-db.sh`; the PGlite side loads the committed `benchmarks/data/dump-small.sql`. The two see the same data only if that remote is what `dump-small.sql` was made from. The package's script is `test:pg`, not the `pnpm test` the README says. In CI, `codegen-tests.yml` lists `packages/analytics-engine/compat/**` under `paths-ignore`, and no workflow invokes the package; the analytics job in `e2e-tests.yml` runs the browser and pg packages' own integration tests, not a cross-store comparison.

**What it predicts.** A change that makes the two stores disagree (a SQL dialect difference, an ordering change, a timestamp-handling fix in one store only) passes CI. Parity claims about the stores are as good as the last time someone ran `test:pg` locally against a matching dataset. The same directory's `src/query-list.ts` deep-compares two GraphQL endpoints and is a manual dev-versus-prod tool, with Heroku URLs in the README.

{"updatedAt":"2026-09-29T15:41:16.028Z","description":"Reuse is most useful when the search indexer can reliably find the text inside the existing JSON structure."}

{"content":"A search feature can start from data that a client rebuild already produces, avoiding a separate content-export step. The team proposed to “reuse the existing JSON version from client rebuilds for the search function,” potentially without further stripping it down.\n\nThis approach holds if the rebuild JSON contains the searchable content in a form the search implementation can traverse. It does not guarantee a low-effort implementation: the team reported difficulty identifying the actual text path in a complex JSON file while testing Fuse.js. If nested content is hard to locate, additional transformation or indexing work may still be needed. Reuse is therefore a plausible shortcut, not proof that the data is search-ready.","updatedAt":"2026-09-29T15:41:16.028Z"}

{"title":"A synchronized inbox can bridge remote webhook receipt to local processing.","updatedAt":"2026-09-29T15:44:28.597Z"}
{"updatedAt":"2026-09-29T15:44:28.597Z","description":"A remote receiver can accept callbacks and synchronization can carry them to a local document, where a processor performs configured actions."}

{"content":"A webhook does not have to trigger local work at the point of receipt. The proposed design accepts calls on a remote drive, forwards them through synchronization to a local “inbox” document, and has a processor listen to that document and execute configured actions. The meeting describes “using a remote drive as a webhook receiver and leveraging the synchronization algorithm to forward webhook calls to a local ‘inbox’ document,” followed by a processor that “would listen to an inbox document and execute configured actions for incoming messages.”\n\nThis architecture applies when a remote receiver is reachable but the desired workflow uses a local drive. It depends on synchronization delivering inbox updates and requires duplicate-action protection, which the participants explicitly identified as a concern. It predicts that receipt and action execution can be handled by separate components, but the meeting records a proposal rather than a verified implementation.","updatedAt":"2026-09-29T15:44:28.597Z"}
{"title":"The Powerhouse Analytics Engine stores time-series as value-interval triples instead of value-time tuples enabling delta and interpolation queries","updatedAt":"2026-08-14T12:34:48.000Z"}
{"updatedAt":"2026-08-14T12:34:48.000Z","description":"Series values have start and end times (not just a point), supporting interval interpolation, running totals, and delta calculations."}

{"content":"The Powerhouse Analytics Engine is a TypeScript time-series analytics system with optional GraphQL interface, designed to run anywhere (browsers, servers, CLI). Unlike typical time-series databases that store `(time, value)` tuples, it stores `(value, start, end)` intervals, enabling interpolation functions (default: constant) and first-class delta queries. `AnalyticsSeries` are the individual metric values; `AnalyticsDimension` objects decorate series with `name` and `path` information for cross-series querying and aggregation. Paths are `/`-delimited strings determining query specificity (e.g., `/atlas/mip40/MIP40c3SP61`). LOD (level of detail) controls aggregation across dimensions; granularity (total/annual/quarterly/monthly/weekly/daily/hourly) controls time aggregation. Data cannot be input through GraphQL, only through the TypeScript API.","updatedAt":"2026-08-14T12:34:48.000Z"}
{"title":"Analytics dimension paths use slash-delimited hierarchies with LOD parameter controlling aggregation specificity across dimensions","updatedAt":"2026-08-14T12:34:49.000Z"}
{"updatedAt":"2026-08-14T12:34:49.000Z","description":"Paths like /atlas/mip40/MIP40c3SP61 determine query scope; LOD 0 groups all results, increasing LOD increases aggregation specificity."}

{"content":"In the Analytics Engine, `AnalyticsDimension` objects have a `path` field using `/`-delimited hierarchical strings (like URIs). Querying with path `/atlas/mip40` matches all dimensions starting with that prefix. The LOD (level of detail) parameter controls result aggregation: LOD 0 groups all results into a single value; LOD 1 groups by the first path segment; LOD 2 by the first two segments, etc. LOD greater than the number of path parts appends `/*` wildcards but returns the same results as the highest meaningful level. Best practice: start with general queries (high LOD, broad path) and narrow down to specific paths and lower LODs for particular metrics. There will be thousands/millions of series objects but far fewer dimension objects.","updatedAt":"2026-08-14T12:34:49.000Z"}

{"title":"Safe-merge beats overwrite when re-syncing externally sourced documents.","updatedAt":"2026-10-02T14:19:07.000Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-08-21T15:40:00.000Z","description":"Gate each update on the target still being editable per its own model status and on its revision matching the one recorded after our last write; otherwise flag for human review rather than writing."}

{"content":"A sync that repeatedly writes a document from an external source faces one question on every event after the first: has a human touched the target since we last wrote it? Blanket overwrite answers "assume not" and is wrong in the only case that matters — the case where someone corrected the machine's output.

The pattern is to gate every update on two conditions, and to write only when both hold:

1. **The target is still editable according to its own model's status.** A document that has moved into a reviewed, approved or issued state has left the machine's jurisdiction; its own lifecycle says so, and the sync should respect that boundary rather than reason about it.
2. **The target's current revision equals the revision recorded after our last write.** If the numbers match, nothing has happened to the document that we did not do. If they diverge, something else wrote — and we do not know what.

When either gate fails, the update is not applied and not dropped: it is flagged for human review, so the divergence surfaces as a decision rather than as silence.

**The revision check is a weaker instrument than per-field provenance, and worth being explicit about why.** Per-field provenance would record, for each field, who last set it, letting a sync update the fields a human never touched while leaving the edited ones alone. The revision heuristic cannot do that. It is coarse: one human edit anywhere in the document freezes the whole document against automated update, which means it will refuse writes that would have been perfectly safe. That is the trade being made deliberately — the failure mode of the coarse check is a refused write that a human then resolves, and the failure mode of overwrite is destroyed human work. Only one of those is recoverable.

Applied in the Paperless x Powerhouse sync (21 Aug 2026), where the recorded revision lives in the sync document alongside the rest of the audit trail.

## Connections

- **RELATES_TO [[Idempotent external ingestion stores the dedup set and the watermark in document state, not in worker memory]]** — the revision recorded after our last write *is* a watermark, and that note says where it has to live: in document state, so a restarted worker still knows what it wrote.
- **RELATES_TO [[Reactor operation-based model handles concurrent edits natively; no CRDT is needed]]** — the reactor merges concurrent op streams without losing operations, but op-level merge cannot tell an external writer that a particular field carries a human's correction. Structural merge safety does not imply semantic merge safety, which is why the sync needs its own gate.
- **RELATES_TO [[Generic attachment-slot discovery needs ranking, not first-match]]** — both are the same failure class: a write that passes every validation and is therefore wrong invisibly.

## Methodology grounding

This is the read/write asymmetry of [[automated detection is always safe because it only reads state while automated remediation risks content corruption]] applied to an integration rather than to vault maintenance: a refused sync costs attention, an unwanted overwrite costs content, and the corruption is invisible afterwards because the overwritten state becomes what everything downstream trusts. The decision to flag rather than write when a gate fails is [[the fix-versus-report decision depends on determinism reversibility and accumulated trust]] resolving toward report, because the condition that failed is precisely the one that told us the outcome was still deterministic. That the coarse check is knowingly accepted in place of per-field attribution is the gap named by [[provenance tracks where beliefs come from]] — without per-field origin, the system cannot distinguish what it wrote from what it was told.","updatedAt":"2026-08-21T15:50:00.000Z"}
{"title":"Content-hash gating avoids paying for redundant AI extraction.","updatedAt":"2026-10-02T14:14:02.000Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-08-21T15:40:00.000Z","description":"Source systems fire document-updated events for metadata-only changes like tags and titles, so hashing the OCR text and skipping extraction when it is unchanged removes most repeat LLM cost."}

{"content":"In a document-sync pipeline the expensive step is the model call: extracting structured fields from OCR text costs real money per document, and unlike the rest of the pipeline that cost does not amortise.

The trap is that "document updated" from a source system does not mean "the document's content changed". In Paperless-ngx, a Document Updated event fires when someone adds a tag, renames the document, changes its correspondent or moves its storage location. None of those change a single character of the OCR text the extractor reads. A pipeline that reacts to the event by re-extracting pays the full model cost for an input it has already processed, and — because model output is not deterministic — may also produce a slightly different answer, generating a spurious update downstream.

The fix is to hash the extractor's actual input, not the event: store the hash of the OCR text alongside the extraction result, and on each event compare the incoming text's hash against the stored one. Equal hash means the extractor's input is unchanged, so the previous result still stands and the model call is skipped entirely. Metadata-only edits — which are the majority of update events in a system where humans curate tags — then cost nothing.

Note what the hash is taken over: it must cover exactly the bytes fed to the model. Hashing a whole API payload would include the metadata that just changed and defeat the purpose; hashing a document ID or modification timestamp would never match. The gate works only when its key is the extractor's input.

## Connections

- **BUILDS_ON [[Semantic search over documents runs on PGlite's vector extension with content-hash re-embed skipping]]** — that note establishes content-hash skipping for embedding; this one carries the same mechanism to LLM extraction, where the skipped operation costs money per call and returns non-deterministic output, so the gate buys more than a saved cycle.
- **RELATES_TO [[Paperless-ngx can push document events to external systems, so integrations do not need polling]]** — the Document Updated trigger described there is exactly what produces the redundant events this gate absorbs; adopting push is what makes the gate necessary.
- **RELATES_TO [[Idempotent external ingestion stores the dedup set and the watermark in document state, not in worker memory]]** — the stored hash is the same kind of durable comparison key, and it must survive a worker restart for the same reason.

## Methodology grounding

This is compare-before-acting from [[idempotent maintenance operations are safe to automate because running them twice produces the same result as running them once]], with a specific reason for wanting it: the operation being made repeat-safe is expensive and non-deterministic, so the cost of running it twice is both a bill and a spurious diff, not merely a wasted cycle.","updatedAt":"2026-08-21T15:50:00.000Z"}

{"title":"Drive analytics writes one counter per operation with four dimension paths, so a question like which files were moved last week is a dimension filter rather than a scan","updatedAt":"2026-09-03T07:43:18.654Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-09-03T07:43:18.654Z","description":"DriveOperations counts 1 per operation across drive, operation, target and actionType dimensions. Action types map many operations onto CREATED, DUPLICATED, UPDATED, MOVED and REMOVED."}

{"content":"The `drive-analytics` package ships two processors — `DriveAnalyticsProcessor` for document-drive operations and `DocumentAnalyticsProcessor` for individual document operations — both converting operations into time-series points with dimensions.

The primary metric is deliberately trivial: **`DriveOperations`, a counter whose value is 1 for each operation**, at per-operation timestamp precision. All the analytical power sits in four dimension paths:

| Dimension | Path format | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drive | `ph/drive/{driveId}/{branch}/{scope}/{revision}` | `ph/drive/abc123/main/global/42` |
| Operation | `ph/drive/operation/{operationType}/{operationIndex}` | `ph/drive/operation/ADD_FILE/5` |
| Target | `ph/drive/target/{targetType}/{targetId}` — `DRIVE` or `NODE` | `ph/drive/target/NODE/file123` |
| Action type | `ph/drive/actionType/{actionType}/{targetId}` | `ph/drive/actionType/CREATED/file123` |

The **action-type dimension is the interpretive one**, folding raw operations into five verbs: `CREATED` (`ADD_FILE`, `ADD_FOLDER`), `DUPLICATED` (`COPY_NODE`), `UPDATED` (`UPDATE_FILE`, `UPDATE_NODE`), `MOVED` (`MOVE_NODE`), `REMOVED` (`DELETE_NODE`). That is what lets a dashboard ask "how much creation happened" without enumerating operation names.

Two operational behaviours: operations are processed in **configurable chunks (default 50)**, and the processor **clears and rebuilds analytics data when processing from index 0** — so a replay from the start is idempotent rather than doubling every count. Analytics data is organised under the source path `ph/drive/{documentId}/{branch}/{scope}`.

None of those depend on the delivery interface.

{"title":"Four analytics stores split by runtime: MemoryAnalyticsStore and KnexAnalyticsStore run everywhere, BrowserAnalyticsStore is browser-only and PostgresAnalyticsStore is server-only","updatedAt":"2026-09-03T07:54:42.099Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-09-03T07:54:42.099Z","description":"MemoryAnalyticsStore loads a WASM Postgres (PGlite) and needs an async init() that is not on IAnalyticsStore; PostgresAnalyticsStore assumes an already-initialized database and adds a dev-only."}

{"content":"| Store | Browser | Node | Bun |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `MemoryAnalyticsStore` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| `BrowserAnalyticsStore` | ✅ | | |
| `KnexAnalyticsStore` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| `PostgresAnalyticsStore` | | ✅ | ✅ |

Two of the four have behaviour worth knowing before choosing.

**`MemoryAnalyticsStore`** is in-memory by way of **a WASM build of Postgres — PGlite**. It requires an asynchronous `await store.init()` for two reasons: downloading and initialising the WASM build when no `PGlite` instance was supplied, and initialising the in-memory database's schema. The initialisation is **idempotent** (existing tables are not recreated), and — importantly — `init()` **is not on the `IAnalyticsStore` interface**, only on the concrete type, so a caller holding the interface cannot initialise it. Both `knex` and `pglite` objects can be passed in, which is how it shares a database with other consumers.

**`PostgresAnalyticsStore`** uses the `pg` package and **assumes a fully-initialised Postgres database already exists** — the opposite contract. It takes a connection string or a `knex` instance, and adds a `raw(sql: string)` method that is *not* on the interface and is explicitly "not intended for production use cases".

Both accept the same optional constructor extras for observability: `queryLogger`, `resultsLogger` and a `profiler`.

{"title":"Analytics dimensions are explored top-down by setting a high level of detail and reading the available paths back before narrowing the select","updatedAt":"2026-09-03T07:54:55.760Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-09-03T07:54:55.760Z","description":"Leave select at the root and lod at 5 to see the sub-paths under a filter, then narrow the select to the path you need. Metric and granularity names are case-sensitive."}

{"content":"The analytics engine's dimensional model is hierarchical (paths like `atlas/scopes/SUP/I/PHOENIX/`), and the documented way to work with it is **general first, then narrow**:

> "Looking at the dimension section in the filter options: to see available sub paths for the budget, leave the `select: "atlas"` and `lod` as 5. With `lod: 5` you'll be able to see the different paths available under your defined filter. Then, later, you can apply a more detailed path in the `select: "atlas/..."` path that will suit your needs."

```json
{ "filter": { "dimensions": [ { "name": "budget", "select": "atlas", "lod": 5 } ] } }
```

So `lod` (level of detail) is an **exploration tool** as much as a rollup depth: a query is also how you discover the taxonomy. The same applies to the vocabulary itself — `analytics { metrics }` and `analytics { dimensions { name values { path label description icon } } }` are queries whose whole purpose is to tell you what you may filter on.

Two operational rules from the same page: **upper- and lower-case matter** for metric and granularity names, so a mistyped case returns nothing rather than erroring; and **fetch per specified path** if performance is a concern, rather than pulling a broad subtree.

The guidance on combining dimensions is judgement, not mechanism, and its useful half is the warning: combining dimensions adds depth, but "avoid overly complex combinations that might lead to confusing or inconclusive results."

{"title":"V6 processors receive a flat OperationWithContext list via onOperations instead of grouped strands via onStrands","updatedAt":"2026-08-14T12:36:06.000Z"}
{"updatedAt":"2026-08-14T12:36:06.000Z","description":"The IProcessor interface simplified from strand-based to flat operation-based with per-operation context including global ordinal."}

{"content":"The v6 Reactor replaced `onStrands(strands: InternalTransmitterUpdate[])` with `onOperations(operations: OperationWithContext[])`. Each OperationWithContext destructures as `{ operation, context }` where context has `documentId`, `documentType`, `scope`, `branch`, `ordinal` (global monotonic counter for cross-document ordering), and optional `resultingState` (JSON string). Operation access changed: `operation.type` -> `operation.action.type`, `operation.input` -> `operation.action.input`, `operation.timestamp` -> `operation.action.timestampUtcMs`. Steady-state live routing delivers each matching operation once, in global-ordinal order, but delivery is not exactly-once overall: backfill and replay are an explicit part of the processor contract, so idempotence guards (`clearSource` / `index === 0` rebuilds) are still recommended. The manager pages through history via `operationIndex.getSinceOrdinal(lastOrdinal)` when a factory registers against a drive that already has history, after a restart to replay the gap missed while the reactor was down, and when `tracked.retry()` re-activates an errored processor and re-runs backfill. Cursors persist in the `ProcessorCursor` table keyed by `processorId`, and on startup the manager rehydrates them and catch-up replays the gap. Factory signature changed from `(driveId: string)` to `(driveHeader: PHDocumentHeader, processorApp?: ProcessorApp)` with outer parameter changing from direct dependencies to `IProcessorHostModule`.\n\n_Corrected 2026-08-13 against Powerhouse v6.2.2-dev.45._","updatedAt":"2026-08-14T12:36:06.000Z"}

{"title":"Currency is a filter field on an analytics query rather than a dimension, so comparing two currencies means two queries whose results are labelled separately","updatedAt":"2026-09-03T07:55:03.009Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-09-03T07:55:03.009Z","description":"The Sky dashboard's model sets currency to DAI or MKR in the filter object; the guidance is to be consistent per query and to run separate queries when comparing, since the choice changes what the."}

{"content":"In the Sky dashboard's analytics model, **currency is a top-level filter field**, not a dimension:

```json
{ "filter": { "start": "2023-01-01", "end": "2024-01-01", "granularity": "total",
              "metrics": ["Budget"], "dimensions": [{ "name": "budget", "select": "atlas", "lod": 3 }],
              "currency": "MKR" } }
```

Three consequences the page draws out:

- **Be consistent per query.** A currency is set once for the whole query, so every row in a series is in that currency.
- **Comparing currencies means separate queries.** "If your analysis involves comparing data across both DAI and MKR, ensure that separate queries are made for each currency and the results are appropriately labeled and distinguished." There is no cross-currency series.
- **The choice changes the question.** DAI "provides a stable measure for financial planning and tracking" while MKR "offers insights into governance and decision-making aspects of the ecosystem" — so the same metric in two currencies answers two different questions rather than the same one in two units.

The modelling lesson generalises beyond Sky: a unit of account belongs in the filter when a series must be internally consistent, and in a dimension only when mixed-unit rows are meaningful. The engine returns `unit` on every row, which is what makes the distinction checkable rather than assumed.

{"title":"Reactor metrics are derived from six event-bus events, so every counter and histogram is traceable to the event that produced it","updatedAt":"2026-09-03T07:43:12.836Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-09-03T07:43:12.836Z","description":"Queue, executor, job-lifecycle, read-model, event-bus and sync families under the @powerhousedao/reactor meter. JOB_WRITE_READY records executor duration and operations generated; JOB_READ_READY."}

{"content":"Every metric uses the meter name `@powerhousedao/reactor`, and units follow OpenTelemetry semantic conventions in UCUM — curly-brace annotations like `{job}`, `{operation}`, `{event}` and `{remote}` are dimensionless counts, `ms` is a duration.

The families:

- **Queue** — `reactor.queue.jobs.enqueued` / `.dequeued` / `.completed` (READ_READY) / `.failed` (permanently) as counters, plus observable gauges `reactor.queue.depth` (pending jobs across all queues) and `reactor.queue.executing`.
- **Executor** — `reactor.executor.job.duration` (histogram, ms, RUNNING → WRITE_READY, attribute `job.success`), `reactor.executor.active_jobs`, `reactor.executor.total_processed` (attribute `job.success`), `reactor.executor.operations_generated`.
- **Read model** — `reactor.readmodel.index.duration` (histogram, WRITE_READY → READ_READY).
- **Event bus** — `reactor.eventbus.events.emitted` with an `event.type` attribute.
- **Sync** — `reactor.sync.remotes` (active remote count) and `reactor.sync.dead_letters.added` with a `remote.name` attribute.

What makes the taxonomy genuinely useful is the event-mapping table: each metric is recorded from a named event, so a gap in a metric is a gap in an event.

| Event | Code | Records |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `JOB_PENDING` | 10001 | `queue.jobs.enqueued` |
| `JOB_RUNNING` | 10002 | `queue.jobs.dequeued` |
| `JOB_WRITE_READY` | 10003 | `executor.job.duration`, `total_processed`, `operations_generated` |
| `JOB_READ_READY` | 10004 | `readmodel.index.duration`, `job.total.duration`, `queue.jobs.completed` |
| `JOB_FAILED` | 10005 | `queue.jobs.failed`, `total_processed`, `job.total.duration` |
| `DEAD_LETTER_ADDED` | 20004 | `sync.dead_letters.added` |

Every one of them also increments `eventbus.events.emitted`.

{"title":"The relational layer wraps PGlite in Kysely and turns a processor's schema into typed live-query hooks with automatic parameter memoization","updatedAt":"2026-09-03T07:38:50.632Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-09-03T07:38:50.632Z","description":"createProcessorQuery<Schema>() builds a hook from a query callback; static and parameterised forms are both supported, and parameters that change over time are memoized so an inline object does not."}

{"content":"`@powerhousedao/reactor-browser` ships a high-level relational layer over PGlite: **type-safe operations through Kysely** plus **live queries with real-time updates**. The workflow it documents is three steps — define the database schema as a TypeScript type, create a typed query hook, use it in a component.

`createProcessorQuery<Schema>()` is the factory. It supports **static queries** with no parameters and **parameterised** ones, taking a query callback that receives the Kysely builder, and returns a hook whose result carries loading state. Two ergonomics are called out explicitly:

- **automatic memoization** of parameters, including "parameters that change over time" — so passing an inline object does not re-run the query on every render, which is the classic live-query footgun;
- **automatic optimization** and full type safety from the schema type, so a column rename is a compile error rather than a runtime empty result.

The documented usage range goes from a basic select through conditional queries and custom SQL to complex joins — meaning the escape hatch to raw SQL is part of the design, not an omission.

The layer's reason for existing is the pairing: a processor writes into its namespaced tables, and a component reads the same tables reactively, with the schema type shared between them. That is what makes a relational processor's output usable in a UI without an intermediate API.

{"title":"PGlite-backed analytics is about 1.36x the time of Postgres on 600+ real queries, so the memory store is a genuine alternative rather than a toy","updatedAt":"2026-09-03T07:54:48.032Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-09-03T07:54:48.032Z","description":"Measured against ~200k-record tables. WASM startup costs ~323 ms, 100 inserts 2.08 ms, 200k inserts 4.45 s. Benchmarks run on every publish and results for major releases are kept in the repository."}

{"content":"Because metrics collection is performance-sensitive, the analytics engine ships a benchmark suite comparing its store implementations, **run on every publish** with major-release results kept in the repository.

The headline: `MemoryAnalyticsStore` and `PostgresAnalyticsStore` are "very close in performance, with the Postgres implementation slightly faster in most applications."

**Query-list benchmark** — the 600+ most frequent real-world queries against matching tables of around **200k records**: on average the memory (PGlite) store took about **1.36×** the time of the Postgres store.

**WASM benchmark** — startup and insert cost for the memory store:

| Operation | Ops/sec | Average time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Init | 3 | 323.00 ms |
| 100 inserts | 478 | 2.08 ms |
| 200k inserts | 0 | 4448.10 ms |

Read together, those numbers say something useful about design choices: a **one-off 323 ms** initialisation and a 36% query penalty is a reasonable price for running the same analytics code in a browser with no server — which is exactly the trade the vault's own PGlite-based semantic search makes. The 200k-insert figure is the one to respect: bulk backfill into a WASM database is measured in seconds, so a processor replaying long history should expect it.

{"title":"The analytics engine is a distributed time-series system split into a core interface module and per-backend storage modules for knex, pg and browser","updatedAt":"2026-09-03T07:44:15.506Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-09-03T07:44:15.506Z","description":"core/ holds the primary interface plus query and aggregation components; knex/, pg/ and browser/ are the backing storage engines. Every module extends the root tsconfig in a pnpm workspace."}

{"content":"The `analytics-engine` is described as "a powerful, distributed, time-series analytics system, written in Typescript", and its shape is a module split that mirrors the reactor's storage-agnostic design:

- **`core/`** — the primary interface for interacting with the engine, and the home of the **query and aggregation** components;
- **`knex/`, `pg/`, `browser/`** — the backing **storage engines**.

So the query surface is written once and the persistence is chosen per host: `pg` for a server, `browser` for an in-page store, `knex` for anything else it can reach. That is the same separation the reactor makes between `IOperationStore` and its Kysely implementation, and it is why the analytics hooks in reactor-browser can present the same query API a switchboard uses.

Toolchain notes for anyone working in it: `pnpm` as the package manager, `tsc-watch` as the filewatcher, `vitest` for tests, every module extending the root `tsconfig.json`, and the repository configured as a **pnpm workspace** so `pnpm install` at the root installs for every module and `pnpm test` runs every suite.

{"title":"The relational processor spec names migration injection and a compromised processor as its worst cases, and answers them with per-project database isolation","updatedAt":"2026-09-03T07:31:14.116Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-09-03T07:31:14.116Z","description":"A compromised processor could read document data, alter schema through migration injection, exfiltrate through business logic, or affect its siblings' tables. Mitigations: isolation and audit logs."}

{"content":"The spec's security section is one of the few written threat models in the repository, and its two scenarios are worth knowing because they follow from the shared-database goal.

**Compromised processor instance.** A processor could access sensitive document data from the relational database, **modify database schema through migration injection**, exfiltrate data through malicious business logic, or impact other processors sharing the same database. The stated mitigations: database isolation per project, **migrations validated and signed before execution**, input sanitisation of document operations, and audit logging of database operations.

**Database access compromise.** Unauthorised access could expose all processed document data, modify processor-generated data, or disrupt operations. Mitigations: TLS on all connections, access restricted to processor instances, sensitive data encrypted at rest, encrypted and access-controlled backups.

Two of these are worth flagging as *aspirations rather than observed behaviour* — signed migrations and complete audit trails are listed as measures in a spec whose API description is otherwise out of date, so a reader should verify before relying on either. What is structurally true and independent of the spec's age: a processor runs inside the trust boundary, sees unfiltered operations, and shares a database with its siblings, so "principle of least privilege" for a processor means limiting which **tables** it touches — the namespace — not which documents it sees.

{"content":"A processor implements `IProcessor` with `onOperations(operations: OperationWithContext[])` and `onDisconnect()`. Each `OperationWithContext` pairs an `Operation` (action type, input, index, hash, timestamp) with `OperationContext` (documentId, documentType, scope, branch, ordinal for cross-document ordering, resultingState as JSON). `ProcessorFilter` has optional arrays: `documentType`, `scope`, `branch`, `documentId`. {"title":"Processors are materialised views over the operation log and can be rebuilt by replaying from zero","updatedAt":"2026-08-14T12:35:40.000Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-08-14T12:35:40.000Z","description":"Because a processor only reduces an immutable log, changing its code cannot corrupt the source of truth — drop the read model and replay from operation zero."}

{"content":"## The mental model: a lens, not a store of record

A document's operation log is authoritative but not always convenient. Asking "which todos did Alice complete last week?" should not mean replaying an entire log on every request. That is what processors are for: event-driven handlers that subscribe to the operation stream and maintain a **read model** on the side.

Think of each processor as a materialised view. It:

1. Subscribes to one or more document types (or specific documents).
2. Receives every operation as it is appended, in order, exactly once.
3. Updates its own storage — a table, an index, a counter.

Reducers stay lean; queries stay fast; neither side has to know about the other.

## Why replayability is the important property

A processor's only input is an append-only log it does not own. That makes its output *derived data*, and derived data is disposable. Add a counter, fix an aggregation bug, reshape the output — then drop the processor's state and replay from operation zero. The log never changed; only the lens did.

This is what makes processors forgiving in a way that a schema migration on a mutable table is not. A bad migration destroys information. A bad processor produces a wrong view over information that is still fully intact upstream, so the fix is mechanical rather than archaeological.

## Where the line falls

The division of labour is sharp:

- **Reducer** — "what is this document now?" Validation, state transitions. Must be pure.
- **Processor** — "what else should happen because of that operation?" Aggregates, indexes, notifications, side effects.

Counting completed todos across all history belongs in a processor: doing it in the reducer couples the document's state size to its age. Sending mail on assignment belongs in a processor too, because reducers cannot perform I/O. Rejecting an empty title belongs in the reducer, because that check must run *before* the action becomes an operation.

_Source: apps/academy/docs/academy/02-Learn/06-switchboard/03-processors-and-read-models.mdx (Powerhouse v6.2.2-dev.45)._","updatedAt":"2026-08-14T12:35:40.000Z"}
{"title":"Document calculations belong in pure queries rather than persisted state.","updatedAt":"2026-10-02T14:14:08.000Z"}

{"updatedAt":"2026-10-02T14:14:08.000Z","description":"Storing derived values like invoice totals creates redundancy and recalculation; query functions over state plus optional parameters keep results current without edits."}

{"content":"A derived value need not be stored merely because it is part of the document's business logic. Persisting calculations can create redundant state and trigger excessive recalculation, particularly when results depend on changing external inputs such as timestamps.

In the 2026-03-02 sprint kick-off call, Wouter established that document models should use query functions for calculated values, "taking document state and optional external parameters to avoid excessive recalculations," and the team discussed restructuring read and calculation functions into a separate "queries" folder, apart from state-mutating reducers. The cited example is an invoice with calculated subtotals and totals; the same approach applies whenever a calculation depends on inputs that should not be persisted in the document.

Evidence: "including all calculated values in the document state can lead to excessive recalculations and redundancy, especially when calculations depend on external parameters like timestamps".

Because such a function depends only on the state and the parameters passed to it, a derived result can be recomputed on demand without stale duplicated values. This does not imply that every user choice must be external: an actual default or other intended document change remains a state edit.","updatedAt":"2026-10-02T14:14:08.000Z"}

{"title":"Processors run only on the in-process reactor path — the SharedWorker path silently skips every factory","updatedAt":"2026-08-14T12:35:40.000Z"}
{"updatedAt":"2026-08-14T12:35:40.000Z","description":"Connect logs a warning and skips registration on the worker path, so worker-hosted reactors run no processors today."}

{"content":"The processor documentation carries an explicit "Not stable yet" warning that is easy to miss and expensive to discover empirically: **processors run only on the in-process reactor path.** On the SharedWorker reactor path, processor registration is not bridged — Connect logs a warning and skips every factory (`apps/connect/src/store/reactor.ts`). Worker-hosted reactors do not run processors today.

The failure mode is the worst kind: silent and total. Nothing throws. Your factory builder is never called, `onOperations` never fires, your relational tables stay empty, and the only signal is a console warning. Anything that depends on a processor — a search index, an analytics rollup, a webhook, a follow-up dispatch — simply does not happen.

This also explains the shape of the registration API. The processor manager is deliberately **not** a method on `IReactor`; it lives on the in-process reactor module as `processorManager`. Reaching it requires narrowing on the module kind, which is the code-level expression of the same constraint:

```typescript
const reactorModule =
  reactorClientModule.kind === "browser"
    ? reactorClientModule.reactorModule
    : undefined;

await reactorModule?.processorManager.registerFactory(id, factory);
```

Note the optional chaining. If the reactor is not on the browser in-process path, `reactorModule` is `undefined` and the `registerFactory` call evaporates without complaint.

Practical consequences while this is unstable:

- Verify which path a host actually booted before debugging a processor that "does not run" — check the module kind, not the processor code.
- Treat processor-mediated behavior as unavailable in worker-hosted topologies, and do not build UI that assumes a read model will be populated.
- When you do register, use the package name as the `identifier`; re-registering the same identifier unregisters the prior factory first, so registration is idempotent.

Related but separate: a factory that *throws* is caught, logged as `Factory '<id>' failed for drive '<driveId>'`, and skipped for that drive — registration does not crash.

_Source: apps/academy/docs/academy/04-Reference/01-Reactor/05-Processors.md (Powerhouse v6.2.2-dev.45)._","updatedAt":"2026-08-14T12:35:40.000Z"}

{"title":"One package plugs into all three tiers: the Reactor runs its reducers, Connect renders its editors, Switchboard runs its processors","updatedAt":"2026-08-14T12:35:29.000Z"}
{"updatedAt":"2026-08-14T12:35:29.000Z","description":"You write the logic once and the stack decides where each part executes — there is no per-host variant of a document model."}

{"content":"When you build on Powerhouse you ship one artefact: a package bundling document models (schemas plus reducers), editor components, and processors. You do not ship a browser build and a server build. The same package plugs into the whole stack, and each tier picks up the part that belongs to it.

## The division of labour

- The **Reactor** picks up your reducers and runs them whenever an action is dispatched.
- **Connect** renders your editor components so users can interact with documents.
- **Switchboard** runs your processors, which fold the operation stream into read models and expose them over GraphQL.

Three consumers, one bundle. As the Academy puts it: you write the logic once, and the stack decides where it executes.

## Why it matters

This is what makes "install a package" a meaningful unit of capability rather than a partial delivery. A package is not a library you then have to wire into three places — it is a complete vertical slice. Adding it to a deployment adds the document type, its UI, and its derived data at once, and nothing about the package changes depending on where it lands.

## The mental model

Read the package as declarative and the tiers as interpreters. The package says *what* exists: this is the schema, these are the legal transitions, this is how it looks, this is what should be derived from it. Each tier reads the portion addressed to it and ignores the rest. Connect never looks at your processors; Switchboard never mounts your React components.

## What follows from it

The routing is by module kind, not by configuration, so there is no manifest step where you tell each host which parts to take — and no opportunity for the three tiers to disagree about which version of the logic they are running. It also sets the boundary for where code belongs: UI concerns in the editor module, state transitions in the reducer, derived reads in the processor. Put something in the wrong module and it simply never executes, because no tier is looking for it there.

_Source: apps/academy/docs/academy/02-Learn/02-architecture/01-the-big-picture.mdx (Powerhouse v6.2.2-dev.45)._","updatedAt":"2026-08-14T12:35:29.000Z"}

The division of labour is sharp:

- **Reducer** — "what is this document now?" Validation, state transitions. Must be pure.
- **Processor** — "what else should happen because of that operation?" Aggregates, indexes, notifications, side effects.

Counting completed todos across all history belongs in a processor: doing it in the reducer couples the document's state size to its age. Sending mail on assignment belongs in a processor too, because reducers cannot perform I/O. Rejecting an empty title belongs in the reducer, because that check must run *before* the action becomes an operation.

# Best practices

### GraphQL

**Start general, end with detailed queries.** In the case you want to find a specific number for a specific metric and dimension, the rule of thumb is to start general in the filter definitions and slowly start cutting down the paths to a particular team or budget period.

For example: Looking at the dimension section in the filter options: To see available sub paths for the budget, leave the select: "atlas" and lod as 5 . With lod:5 you'll be able to see the different paths available under your defined filter. Then, later you can apply a more detailed path in the select: "atlas/..." path that will suit your needs.

```graphql
{
  "filter": {
  ...
    "dimensions": [
      {
        "name": "budget",
        "select": "atlas",
        "lod": 5
      }
    ],
   ...
  }
}
```

**Follow upper case, lower case rules.** To make sure to get the results you require, you must follow the upper or lower case styling for defining the metrics and granularity. To see the available metrics and dimensions just use the referenced queries. For granularity, check the above granularity section for the different types.

**Fetch per specified path** if performance is an issue.

### Guidelines for selecting and combining dimensions

1. **Understand the Purpose of Analysis**  
   Before selecting dimensions, clarify the objective of your analysis. Are you looking to track expenses for a specific project, analyze budget utilization, or examine transaction patterns? Your objective will guide which dimensions are most relevant.

2. **Choose Relevant Dimensions**  
   Select dimensions that align with your analytical goals. For instance, use the 'Project' dimension for project-based financial tracking or 'Wallet' for blockchain transaction analysis.

3. **Combining Dimensions for Depth**  
   Combine multiple dimensions to gain more nuanced insights. For example, you might combine 'Budget' and 'Category' to understand how different categories of expenses contribute to overall budget utilization within a specific area.

4. **Hierarchy and Path Considerations**  
   Pay attention to the hierarchical structure in dimension paths. For instance, paths like atlas/scopes/SUP/I/PHOENIX/ suggest a structured breakdown that can be crucial for detailed analysis.

5. **Utilize Descriptions for Context**  
   Where available, use the descriptions provided with dimension values to understand the context and relevance of each dimension to your analysis. This is particularly helpful in dimensions with null labels, where the path and description provide critical information.

6. **Avoid Over-Complication**  
   While combining dimensions can provide depth, avoid overly complex combinations that might lead to confusing or inconclusive results. Stick to combinations that directly serve your analysis objectives.

7. **Use Icons for Quick Reference**  
   Where icons are available, they can be used as a quick visual reference to identify different dimensions or categories, particularly in user interfaces where rapid identification is beneficial.

8. **Experiment and Iterate**  
   Don't hesitate to experiment with different combinations of dimensions to see which provide the most meaningful insights. The flexibility of the dimensions allows for various permutations and combinations to suit diverse analytical needs.

9. **Stay Updated**  
   Keep abreast of any changes or additions to the dimensions within the analytics engine, as this can impact ongoing and future analyses.

Summary
Wouter - Powerhouse and Apeiron - Powerhouse discussed the Atlas Explorer demo on August 1st, including its full-text search and preparing it to be AI-friendly. They also addressed full-text search improvements, an MCP API, and Acra integration with UI changes. Wouter - Powerhouse, teep - Powerhouse, and liberuum - Powerhouse reviewed invoice editor tasks, billing statement fixes, invoice validation, and Request Finance configuration, with liberuum - Powerhouse explaining API key security and webhook configuration. Wouter - Powerhouse and liberuum - Powerhouse discussed invoice document processing, the reliance on shared drives for webhooks, and the need for architectural clean-up to allow configurable drive selection. Wouter - Powerhouse proposed a workshop to configure webhooks for local drives using a remote drive as a receiver and building a messaging system based on document synchronization, while also discussing upcoming meetings and tasks with liberuum - Powerhouse.

Details
Demo Scenario for Atlas Explorer Wouter - Powerhouse initiated a discussion about the demo scenario scheduled for August 1st, emphasizing the importance of quick rollouts for small features based on stakeholder feedback (00:00:00). Apeiron - Powerhouse clarified that the demo would involve navigating the Atlas Explorer and utilizing its full-text search feature, which is already implemented. They noted that stakeholder feedback regarding showing the text content in the preview has been acknowledged and is a potential next step (00:03:43).
AI-Friendly Atlas Explorer Apeiron - Powerhouse outlined the second step of the demo, which involves preparing Atlas to be AI-friendly by determining the easiest way for AI bots to parse its content. This research is currently being conducted by Yel, the integrations engineer (00:05:02) (00:08:42). Potential approaches include HTML scraping or generating a Markdown file, with a previous demo scenario already incorporating HTML page generation for governance (00:08:42).
Full-Text Search Improvements Wouter - Powerhouse inquired about the use of libraries for the full-text search feature, suggesting that such libraries could sort search results by matching score and potentially enable fuzzy matching for different spellings (00:06:21). While the current search function is operational, Apeiron - Powerhouse acknowledged that it can be improved and will follow up with the team regarding the libraries (00:07:30). Both Wouter - Powerhouse and Apeiron - Powerhouse agreed that incorporating snippets into the search results is a more crucial improvement than sorting or fuzzy matching (00:08:42).
MCP API and Integration Hub Apeiron - Powerhouse mentioned the potential for an MCP API for the entire Atlas, which could serve as an elegant access point for LLMs. Wouter - Powerhouse suggested holding off on the MCP API for now to avoid duplicate work, as the core app team is also building an MCP endpoint (00:09:38). Wouter - Powerhouse proposed creating an "integrations hub drive" on Switchboard to configure all API keys and settings, avoiding the need for individual users to configure their own (00:41:50).
Acra Integration and UI Changes Wouter - Powerhouse discussed integrating the Atlas Explorer with Acra, suggesting a small integration point in the user interface to return to Acra (00:12:16). They proposed moving the "collapse all" and "expand all" buttons next to the search bar and adding the Acra logo to the top right corner, making it optional and configurable in terms of logo and URL (00:13:38). Willow Olive confirmed that this logo would serve as a backlink to the organization's homepage on Acra (00:16:56).
Invoice Editor and Billing Statement Fixes Wouter - Powerhouse and teep - Powerhouse reviewed open tasks related to the invoice editor and O admin overview, specifically the Request Finance integration and generating billing statements (00:16:56). liberuum - Powerhouse reported fixing an issue with slug creation for billing statements and confirmed that the Request Finance integration has been fixed since the demo day (00:19:28). The Request Finance issue was traced to the production API key being linked to an incorrect email, which has since been corrected (00:20:40).
Invoice Validation and Request Finance Configuration Wouter - Powerhouse and liberuum - Powerhouse discussed invoice validation rules, ensuring that essential fields like issue date are filled before an invoice is issued (00:27:22). They also addressed the configuration for Request Finance, confirming that the API key and a specific email address are required (00:28:18). Wouter - Powerhouse suggested moving the Request Finance email address to a setting next to the API key to avoid dependency on the email filled out in the invoice itself (00:34:06).
API Key Security and Document Models liberuum - Powerhouse explained that the API key for Request Finance is protected by calling a GraphQL endpoint from Switchboard rather than directly from the browser (00:36:28). Wouter - Powerhouse supported this approach until encrypted secrets are available client-side (00:38:01). Wouter - Powerhouse also proposed creating specific document models for each integration (e.g., Request Finance, Gnosis Safe, Google Cloud) to provide more structure and improved semantics, rather than a single generic key format (00:45:26).
Webhook Configuration and Security Wouter - Powerhouse and liberuum - Powerhouse discussed the webhook listener setup, which allows Switchboard to receive data from external services like Alchemy (00:43:14) (00:51:01). Wouter - Powerhouse emphasized the importance of adding a secret to the webhook for security purposes and making the webhook URL more specific to prevent unauthorized calls. They also discussed how to integrate this secret into the integration configuration list (00:53:27).
Invoice Document Processing liberuum - Powerhouse explained the process of updating a document's status to "payment received" when data matches local and token executed transactions on Base. This process involves using a switchboard function to access the Powerhouse drive, identify the invoice document type, and locate the invoice number (00:58:58).
Shared vs. Local Drives for Webhooks Wouter - Powerhouse raised a concern about the current setup relying on a local drive for invoice processing, highlighting that it would only work with a shared drive (00:58:58). liberuum - Powerhouse confirmed that the current system was indeed designed for shared drives only, and that a public endpoint is needed for webhooks to function with local drives (01:00:12).
Architectural Clean-up and Configuration Wouter - Powerhouse suggested a need to clean up the architecture to make it configurable, allowing users to select which drive they use. They emphasized that webhooks will only work with a remote drive, but noted that this issue is crucial to address as it will apply to all future integrations (01:00:12).
Webhooks and Local Drive Access Wouter - Powerhouse proposed a feature for Veter to forward webhook calls to local drives, while liberuum - Powerhouse questioned if backend restructuring would allow direct access to local drives through a browser reactor. Wouter - Powerhouse clarified that the main issue is the callback for webhooks, as a local host isn't publicly available to receive them directly (01:01:07).
Workshop for Webhook Solutions Wouter - Powerhouse proposed scheduling a workshop to figure out a systematic way of configuring webhooks, even for local drives. They suggested using a remote drive as a webhook receiver and leveraging the synchronization algorithm to forward webhook calls to a local "inbox" document (01:02:21).
Messaging System for Webhooks Wouter - Powerhouse elaborated on building a messaging system based on document synchronization, where a processor would listen to an inbox document and execute configured actions for incoming messages. This system would be agnostic to the webhook call's origin, though they noted the need to ensure actions are not applied twice due to synchronization (01:03:34).
Upcoming Meetings and Tasks Wouter - Powerhouse highlighted upcoming discussions, including the Atlas demo with the DSP team and a "scope of work v2" meeting. They asked liberuum - Powerhouse to schedule a call with apparent to define the scope of work and wireframes for the latter (01:04:47).

Suggested next steps
liberuum - Powerhouse will add an inbox document, subscribe to it to receive forwarded web hook calls, and write a processor that listens to the inbox document.
liberuum - Powerhouse will ensure that the solution for applying web hook calls does not get applied twice.
Wouter - Powerhouse and liberuum - Powerhouse will schedule a workshop to figure out a systematic way of configuring a remote drive as a web hook receiver, using the synchronization algorithm to forward the web hook calls.


Summary
Apeiron - Powerhouse, Wouter - Powerhouse, Liberuum - Powerhouse, and Frank - Powerhouse discussed query definitions for Acra, focusing on breaking down existing state JSON fields into network-specific data fields and improving GraphQL queries for fetching documents across drives. They also addressed the rework of the network profile and homepage, including displaying "active RFPs" and roadmaps, and decided on a builder profile document model and a complex read model to consolidate builder-related data from various sources. The participants concluded with plans to proceed with implementing "find documents" within the document model subgraphs, with further GraphQL requirements to be addressed in future meetings.

Details
Query Definitions for Acra Apeiron - Powerhouse initiated a discussion on query definitions for Acra, emphasizing the need to break down existing state JSON fields into network-specific data fields. Wouter - Powerhouse suggested prioritizing this topic and confirmed that the core development team is working on a new GraphQL interface to fetch documents across drives, which would eliminate the need for custom queries for network profiles. Liberuum - Powerhouse highlighted that a direct link between network profiles, workstreams, and RFPs is needed, and Wouter - Powerhouse proposed changing the client section of the editor to a selector for network profile documents, defaulting to the one in the same drive.
Network Profile and Homepage Rework Wouter - Powerhouse outlined several tasks related to the network profile and homepage. This included reworking the homepage to display a summarized network profile at the top, replacing the client ID input in the workstream editor with a network profile link, and updating the sidebar to show a static label "Network Profile" with a specified icon. Liberuum - Powerhouse suggested a user flow where creating a network profile is the first step before any other documents can be created.
Proposals and RFPs Display Apeiron - Powerhouse questioned showing proposals on the homepage, leading to a discussion about displaying "active RFPs" instead, specifically those in "pre-work RFC" or "open for proposals" status. Wouter - Powerhouse identified that the relevant information to display for RFPs includes budget range and submission deadline, and suggested changes to the Acra front-end design, such as removing the "details" link and adding a button for viewing details.
Cross-Drive Document Fetching Frank - Powerhouse joined the discussion, understanding the need for a subgraph to fetch documents from different drives. Wouter - Powerhouse confirmed that the goal is to fetch collections of documents directly tied to a document type using standard queries across all drives. They also discussed the limitations of the current `find documents` query in GraphQL regarding type information, aiming for a typed equivalent.
GraphQL Query Enhancements Frank - Powerhouse and Wouter - Powerhouse discussed enhancing GraphQL queries for fetching documents. Frank - Powerhouse suggested changing the existing `get documents` query to `find documents` and marking the former as deprecated, while ensuring it still provides typed information. Wouter - Powerhouse agreed to this approach, emphasizing that the `find documents` query should have a fixed document type and optional drive ID and identifiers.
Scalability of Typed Queries Frank - Powerhouse brought up the idea of using GraphQL interfaces for typed queries, which Wouter - Powerhouse acknowledged as ideal but raised concerns about scalability with a large number of document types. Despite these concerns, Wouter - Powerhouse agreed to proceed with implementing `find documents` within the document model subgraphs as a starting point, acknowledging that further optimization might be needed in the future.
PH Document Result Page and GraphQL Wouter - Powerhouse and Frank - Powerhouse discussed the PH document result page as a typed version of the return value of `find documents`. Frank - Powerhouse clarified that it is typed on the document model subgraph, and Wouter - Powerhouse requested a link to the relevant issue for reference. They agreed to keep further GraphQL requirements for future meetings.
Acra Homepage Proposals Section Wouter - Powerhouse outlined updates for the Acra homepage's proposal section, specifying that the budget would become a budget range, the deadline would be a submission deadline, and a button would replace the experience level details link. They also noted that the "road map" title should adapt to "road maps" if multiple are present. Apeiron - Powerhouse confirmed these updates, including adding a submission deadline and ensuring proposals are visible only if a workstream is open for proposals.
Roadmap Display and Sorting Wouter - Powerhouse and Apeiron - Powerhouse determined that roadmaps shown in the roadmap section should be for workstreams with "awarded" or "in progress" statuses, not "open for proposals" as that relates to proposals. They concluded that roadmaps should be sorted by the final milestone delivery target, as roadmaps themselves do not have direct dates. Apeiron - Powerhouse summarized that active roadmaps will only show for awarded and in-progress workstreams and be sorted by the final milestone delivery target.
Roadmap Progress and Finances Wouter - Powerhouse noted that overall roadmap progress is not currently available in the document model at the roadmap level, only at the milestone level, and decided to postpone implementing roadmap progress calculation due to its complexity. They also decided to add finances as a placeholder but to wait for a specific team member's return before addressing it further.
Wallet and Builder Data Wouter - Powerhouse and Apeiron - Powerhouse agreed that wallets are straightforward, requiring fields for name, address, explore URL, and balances with currency and amount. They identified builders as a more complex area, as they are platform-wide and need to be tied to networks.
Builder Profile Document Model Wouter - Powerhouse proposed creating a "builder profile" document model to reference builders, distinguishing it from individual contributors and ensuring it is a team profile. This model would include fields like PH ID, slug, name, icon, and description. Liberuum - Powerhouse raised concerns about where this builder profile document would live.
Updating Scope of Work Contributors Wouter - Powerhouse suggested updating the scope of work contributors to use the new builder profile document type, which would involve replacing existing agent types with a PH ID selector linking to the builder profile. The contributors list would display a link to the builder profile page within the network's context, constructed using the builder slug or ID.
Builder Read Model and Database Structure Wouter - Powerhouse explained the necessity of a read model for builders to efficiently gather data from various sources. This read model would listen to changes in scope of work documents and builder profile documents to consolidate information and maintain up-to-date details. The database structure for this read model would include `builder_profiles`, `skills`, `builder_skills`, and `builder_networks` tables.
Complex Read Model Relationships Wouter - Powerhouse elaborated on the complex read model for builders, which needs to combine data from builder profiles, scopes of work, and workstream documents. The read model would also consider the status of scopes of work (initial, alternative, active proposals) to determine the highest role for a builder within a workstream. This read model is crucial for providing a read-optimized storage solution, preventing computationally expensive queries.
Read Model Location and Purpose Liberuum - Powerhouse inquired about the setup location for the read model and builder team profile document model. Wouter - Powerhouse suggested tying the read model to the network admin and placing the builder profile in a separate, generic package, potentially named "Acra user profiles," due to its shared nature across networks. Wouter - Powerhouse emphasized that read models ensure data consistency by listening to the original source of truth for labels, icons, and descriptions, preventing data from becoming outdated.
Read Model Decision Factors Wouter - Powerhouse detailed the deciding factors for using a read model, explaining that it's necessary when combining data from multiple (more than two or three) documents, especially at scale, as generic queries and custom subgraphs become inefficient. Apeiron - Powerhouse acknowledged the complexity of read models but recognized their importance in feeding data to the builder list on Acra.
Data Models and Queries Apeiron - Powerhouse and Wouter - Powerhouse discussed combining data using a bit model when more than one reactor query is needed, specifically more than two or three. Wouter - Powerhouse emphasized avoiding premature optimization while still looking ahead at query performance.
Future Meeting for Expense Reports and Other Queries Wouter - Powerhouse proposed a follow-up session for the next day to discuss expense reports and other queries, including actuals, forecast, and budget, but excluding payments. They asked Apeiron - Powerhouse to review all queries in the meantime.

Suggested next steps
Wouter - Powerhouse will follow up with the core development team to ensure that the network profile get documents query can query across drives and is typed, not using state JSON.
Frank - Powerhouse will create an issue to change the code so that documents can be fetched without the drive ID, mark 'get documents' as deprecated, and add 'find documents' as the new version, using the exact same input as 'find documents' minus the document type option.
liberuum - Powerhouse will check lucide.dev for icons and provide a list.
Frank - Powerhouse will put the link to the issue in the chat to provide a reference.
The group will have another session tomorrow morning to look at expense reports, actuals for every wallet, forecast, and budget.
Apeiron - Powerhouse will look at all the queries.
Wouter - Powerhouse will make sure that all the queries, especially the expense reports, are captured.


Summary
Frank - Powerhouse and Wouter - Powerhouse introduced the new operational database processor feature, which enables relational database access and real-time data synchronization for applications. They demonstrated its generation, configuration, testing, and integration with GraphQL and Connect UI for live data display and queries. Willow Olive presented the new branding for Acra and Vetra, emphasizing their distinct visual styles and user onboarding flows through Renown.

Details
Introduction to Operational Database Processors Frank - Powerhouse introduced the new operational database processor feature, explaining that processors are functions called by the reactor after processing document operations (00:00:00). They elaborated that the operational database processor can access a relational database, specifically Postgress and PG light, and offers features like automatic table registration in a dedicated namespace for conflict avoidance and TypeScript interface generation for type safety (00:01:30). Wouter - Powerhouse added that processors are generally used for building "read models" to query data across multiple documents, especially for search functions, which is crucial for scaling data in the network (00:04:39).
Generating and Configuring the Processor Frank - Powerhouse demonstrated how to generate an operational database processor using the `pnpm generate` command, specifying the processor type and optional document types like "sky atlas scope" and "sky atlas foundation" (00:06:18). They showed that this process creates a new directory with four files: factory, index, migrations, and schema, noting that the schema is generated based on the migration definitions (00:07:33). Frank - Powerhouse also highlighted the ability to define database schemas and the use of Kaisley for constructing database queries with type safety and handling conflicts (00:09:24) (00:13:57).
Processor Logic and Database Interaction Frank - Powerhouse explained the `onStrands` method in the processor, which receives processed operations and the resulting state, allowing for indexing the document's state into the operational store (00:12:26). They demonstrated how the processor filters for specific document types (Atlas scope and foundation) and fetches the global scope (00:10:55). Wouter - Powerhouse summarized that the processor listens to changes in defined Atlas documents, updating the database to include the latest data, which then enables search queries and other database operations (00:13:57).
Testing the Processor Frank - Powerhouse outlined the process of testing the implemented processor by instantiating it without the full reactor setup, using a PG light instance in memory, and running database migrations (00:16:46). They explained that tests can involve passing JSON to the `onStrands` method and then performing database queries to validate the stored state, highlighting the speed of these tests (00:18:17).
GraphQL Interface for Data Access Frank - Powerhouse demonstrated how to generate a subgraph to expose the data through a GraphQL endpoint, building on default templates for type definitions and resolvers (00:18:17). They showed an example GraphQL query for "atlas documents" that returns an interface implemented by "atlas scope document" and "atlas foundation document" types, allowing access to the operational store for selecting or searching documents (00:21:00). Wouter - Powerhouse emphasized that this feature extends the data architecture to traditional working methods, enabling integration with various frontends and APIs (00:22:58).
Live Demo and Data Synchronization Frank - Powerhouse conducted a live demo, creating and modifying documents in Connect, and observing how the changes were reflected in the GraphQL interface and the operational store (00:24:33). They acknowledged a current issue where older data might be present if the local store is not deleted before the demo, but demonstrated filtering and searching capabilities within the GraphQL interface (00:28:25). memo.dev - Powerhouse then took over to show how the same operational data could be accessed and displayed directly within the Connect interface, emphasizing the shared architecture and code between local reactor and browser-based Connect instances (00:30:00).
Connect UI Integration and Live Queries memo.dev - Powerhouse demonstrated implementing search functionality in Connect using the `useTypeQuery` hook, which leverages the database schema for type-safe query building with Kaisley (00:36:00) (00:40:43). They showed how to query data from multiple tables and merge results for display, demonstrating how changes in documents are immediately propagated and updated in the database and reflected live across different Connect instances (00:46:02) (00:48:23). Wouter - Powerhouse highlighted that this real-time update is due to PG light's live query feature, which pushes changes instantly to the search results without requiring a refresh (00:56:23) (00:58:38).
Live Data Updates and Database Integration Wouter - Powerhouse introduced a new framework that enables real-time data synchronization and updates across the platform, emphasizing data completeness, correctness, and liveness through the use of PG Light and live queries (00:59:39). Frank - Powerhouse added that while a local reactor using PG Light is available, GraphQL subscriptions are still needed for broader live updates across platforms like Fusion (01:00:52). The discussion also covered how these live updates would enhance user experience for operational apps and allow for richer data queries spanning multiple documents (01:03:58).
Processor and Database Naming Convention Frank - Powerhouse led a quiz about the new system, confirming the reactor calls the processor and that IndexDB, PostgreSQL, and PG Light can be used. Wouter - Powerhouse suggested renaming the "operational processor" to "relational DB processor" to reflect its current function more accurately, while acknowledging future support for other database types like graph databases and full-text search engines (01:05:32).
Documentation and Future Releases Frank - Powerhouse and memo.dev - Powerhouse confirmed that documentation for the new features, including the Connect site, new hooks, and a migration guide for B3.2, will be available in the Academy, with a release planned for the following week (01:07:09). memo.dev - Powerhouse also noted that some fixes for breaking changes are in a separate branch and can be merged into the main branch (01:09:29).
Branding and User Onboarding for Acra and Vetra Willow Olive presented the new branding for Acra, the decentralized operations platform, and Vetra, the builder platform, noting that Acra will focus on a "flow and vibe" with a colorful, categorized approach, while Vetra will adopt a minimalistic, "building blocks" visual style (01:10:51) (01:13:01). Willow Olive also outlined the user onboarding flows for Acra, which will involve login with Renown and then branching into different funnels for teams, contributors, and service providers (01:09:29) (01:13:01). Wouter - Powerhouse clarified that Renown will serve as the primary identity provider for both Acra and Vetra (01:17:02).
Trademarking and Next Steps Layer Zero confirmed that the logos and names for Powerhouse Acra, Powerhouse Vetra, and Open Source Capitalist are cleared for trademarking in the European database, with no conflicts found (01:18:16). Frank - Powerhouse then concluded the meeting by mentioning the next demo will be on the new admin drive with privacy features and that Jeep will be giving the demo (01:19:23).
