Summary
Dracaena - Powerhouse led discussions on creating a document model and editor with multi-currency and approval support, explored development environment needs, and noted the difficulty for non-developers to use the platform, proposing solutions like example prompts and a task specification layer. Separate speakers presented a "clicker game," an ordering solution for McDonald's created with Powerhouse assistance, and a data architecture document model for Acra, with the latter confirming the use of "skills" from Anthropic to Claude Code for development. Key priorities were set for production readiness, including improving data reliability, performance, and establishing backend processor models for relational databases, with a plan for two releases to manage breaking changes.

Details
Notes Length: Standard
Developing a Document Model and Editor Dracaena - Powerhouse was working on creating a document model, which they identified as the actual business component. They requested the model to include support for multiple currencies, an approval field for each item, and approval for each category. Following the model creation, they then requested an editor for the newly created document.
Exploring Coding and Workflow Changes Dracaena - Powerhouse noted that modern coding involves watching the computer do the job, which they find "very annoying" because it disrupts the flow, but allows for more time on platforms like Twitter. They also explored the concept of multiple approval levels for documents.
Discussions on Hardware Costs and Development Environment The conversation touched upon the cost of a purchase, where the price was estimated at $20,000, which Dracaena - Powerhouse noted was the purchase price, likely requiring a separate subscription for software. They mentioned that a pre-order for a robot, not yet ready, costs $20,000 and is expected to be released next year. Dracaena - Powerhouse also discussed development environment needs, noting the ability to run a "little machine", and instructing a colleague to update editor files directly in the project rather than connecting to EMCP.
Functional AI and Data Visualization Dracaena - Powerhouse mentioned the need to use functional AI for meeting summarization and reports. They discussed using the system to read transactions and interpreted data from CSV, noting that it "knows what to do". The speaker then asked for a donut chart at the bottom of the display to show total cost and highlight items in red if the cost percentage exceeds a specific amount.
Chart Implementation and System Support Dracaena - Powerhouse discussed trying to add a chart to a project, suggesting the use of a chart library and PNPM for installation. They mentioned running into problems on Windows, particularly with WSL, and concluded that the current solution is to either avoid Windows or bring direct support to it.
Travel Budget Document Model Dracaena - Powerhouse presented a travel budget document model, created using code with the aid of the Draena tool. This model includes a budget summary, a diagram to visualize expenses—showing, for example, that 41% of the budget goes to hotel and airport costs—and an input section for users to add details like attendee numbers and event phases. The document model incorporates features such as a drop-down menu for category selection, fields for description and cost per unit, and a calculation type. They also detailed a multi-layer approval process with a status column that tracks if an item is approved, suspended, or rejected, which affects the next steps.
Clicker Game Development An unnamed speaker presented a "clicker game" that they had been developing. The game involves clicking to make gizmos, which can then be used to buy gadgets, and once a player has 10 gadgets, they can build a factory. The factory automates the creation of gizmos, and reaching 50 gadgets allows the player to hire a foreman to further automate gadget production; the end-game involves buying an automaton to collect gizmos from all factories.
McDonald's Ordering Solution Another speaker detailed their work on creating a solution for ordering McDonald's with the help of the Powerhouse team. They used the Claude tool to create local orders, including a no-meat order, and generated a tabular view of individual orders for the team, specifying items for members like Alex and Jordan, including two vegetarian options. The speaker expressed their impression with the ability to get data stored and an API to the data right away, and they requested a cheat sheet for writing prompts.
Data Architecture Document Model for Acra A speaker presented their intention to create a document model to structure and organize data for Acra, a system that uses UI components to fetch data from subgraphs and processors. The speaker's goal was to make this model accessible to analysts and developers. Their approach involves defining the URL path (endpoint) first and then adding the subgraphs and processors that will serve that page, which is a method based on how the DBI team thinks in terms of necessary queries for a page.
Processor and Subgraph Definition in Document Model The presenter elaborated on defining subgraphs by specifying fields and their types, and the corresponding query structure, to be consumed by Acra's front end or other services. They explained that processors are middleware that help consolidate data from various models into a single table, thereby reducing server compute time and facilitating faster queries. The presenter demonstrated adding a table processor, allowing users to build a structure and queries on top of the consolidated data.
Use of Skills in Development The speaker who presented the data architecture document model confirmed using a new feature called "skills" provided by Anthropic to Claude Code. They downloaded specific markdown files, such as "front end design" and one for Playwright testing, which instruct Claude to act in a certain way to help build and self-correct the application. These skills were used, for example, to fix a bug where adding a column to a table was not working. The speaker clarified that the skills are triggered by directly mentioning the skill's MD file in the prompt. They also noted that Skillsmp.com is a community website where one can find and download these open-source MD files.
Progress on Nosis Pay Analytics Tool Dracaena - Powerhouse reported lessons learned from slow progress on an analytics tool for Nosis Pay, which aims to provide bank-like analytics and bank statement export capabilities due to the platform's poor built-in analytics. A key learning was that adding too much complexity to the original schema caused issues with AI-generated operations, leading to a broken global state and a "blank white screen of death". The current functionality allows a user to create a transaction analytics document, choose a CSV file (e.g., from Nois Scan), upload it, and confirm the upload, with the plan to build analytics on top of this data by fetching external data like token values from the chain.
Challenges for Non-Developers and Suggested Solutions Dracaena - Powerhouse observed that it is nearly impossible for non-developers to start using the platform at its current stage, as a deep understanding of all components is necessary to effectively prompt the AI. They proposed two solutions: first, creating a list of example prompts, which should be documented in the academy, and second, a more fundamental solution involving creating a specialized list of tasks from which prompts would be produced. This task specification layer would translate high-level user input (via a form) into the necessary documents and task lists for the AI.
Implementing a Publish Step for Sharing Applications Dracaena - Powerhouse identified the lack of a simple publish step as a missing piece in the overall process for sharing built applications. The proposed solution involves two simple steps: publish and install. Once a document is shared and opened in "our connect," the recipient is prompted to install the provided module, which allows for easy sharing of applications like a forms application.
Codifying Logic for AI Prompting and Boilerplate Generation Dracaena - Powerhouse discussed the concept of giving AI, like C, direct access to logic that codifies the reasons for file layouts and export structures, which helps reduce the reliance on the AI guessing and minimizes hallucinations. This approach would allow the AI to read the logic to understand the necessary file structures and why certain components are default exports. They suggested a "generate boiler plates" command, noting that the AI was able to proceed once it had an empty document model, inferring structures from that point. They provided a detailed example of how a function for making an editor is codified, showing how file paths, variable names, component creation, and typing are made clear for the AI.
Surgical Code Updates and Migration Management Dracaena - Powerhouse highlighted the utility of the codified logic for surgical code updates and migration fixes, demonstrated by the ability to change an editor from a named export to a default export. They mentioned that this process allows for both generating code and fixing migration issues simultaneously when running the generate command. Dracaena - Powerhouse also suggested that the logic used for code generation could be added to the MCP as it remains consistent across projects.
Afternoon Session Agenda and Work Streams The afternoon session was outlined to include a smaller group breakout session focused on governance. The overall work is organized into two parallel streams, with the fundraising demo needing only bug fixing and not core development. The second, crucial stream focuses on production readiness, including performance, reliability, data security, and verifiability.
Powerhouse Game Suite and Mind Sweeper Demo Dracaena - Powerhouse demonstrated a small Powerhouse game suite they are developing for users to "wash their brain" between meetings, starting with a collaborative Mind Sweeper game. They showed how users can select difficulty and play together, and mentioned they are also working on a Zodia game with Claude.
Social Post Coordination Application Demo Dracaena - Powerhouse presented a social post coordination application designed to help organize content for the open source hub. The tool allows speakers to submit their Twitter handles, presentations, and profile pictures, which is then organized into an "organizer view" based on categories. Dracaena - Powerhouse noted the value of forms in general, suggesting that their tool is simple, looks better, and is more functional than using a spreadsheet, envisioning its utility for things like a neighborhood association form.
SNO Growth Model Editor Presentation A SNO growth model editor was presented, built with the help of Frank and Aldas, to guide network organizations through development phases from embryonic hub to decay. The model starts with inputs for an embryonic hub, including a multisig wallet, an MPA, and a legal entity (by default a Swiss association). The goal is for the tool to eventually help users set up specialized hubs and spin off entities based on their operational requirements, such as legal or financial needs, though that functionality is not yet complete.
Discussion on AI Development Tools and Functionality Dracaena - Powerhouse compared their development experience to tools like Replit, aiming for an AI experience similar to ChatGPT but focused on building websites or applications. They noted that while Replit is fast for MVPs and aesthetically pleasing, it struggles with data and turning projects into actual products, falling apart with serious data or APIs. They suggested the next evolution of AI generation should focus on generating high-quality structures that can be reliably built upon.
Need for Integrated Version Control Dracaena - Powerhouse emphasized the necessity of integrating version control within the platform, similar to Git functionalities, so users can easily revert changes after an AI-induced error. They noted that relying on external version control tools is too complicated for users, and that having it built-in would enhance reliability.
Discussion on Political Positioning and Open Source Dracaena - Powerhouse raised the question of whether the organization should take a political stance, noting that open source is often perceived as left-leaning, while Web3 and crypto can be seen as right-leaning. They suggested that the organization's focus on open source and cooperatively owned businesses could be seen as political but should aim to be non-partisan by using balanced terminology and focusing on creating "better stuff" and competing through innovation. Dracaena - Powerhouse argued that creating better, decentralized products is the way to achieve anti-trust goals, rather than relying on existing government structures.
Key Priorities for Breakouts and Production Readiness Dracaena - Powerhouse outlined key practical topics for the team breakouts, including a recap of the past week's developments and the hottest irons in the fire for the next few months. The team should identify key improvements for data reliability and performance. A critical goal by the end of March is to have a data network that can import verifiable services and documents with reliable price data. Another priority is establishing the backend processor models for relational databases, which will allow for building backends, such as a graph that reads from this data.
Plan for Critical Path and Releases The critical path involves achieving production readiness, leading up to the processors and weak models that will be exposed as GraphQL endpoints, which will be used for the Sky Sentinel project. Other teams will continue building specific projects and modules for Drive and Ventra. Dracaena - Powerhouse proposed two releases to manage risky, breaking changes early on, which would allow for fixing issues before the final, stable release, suggesting a timeline that would allow for thorough testing, perhaps around March. The largest release is anticipated to involve switching managers and reactors.
Collaboration with Finance and Business Analysis Team Dracaena - Powerhouse noted that the finance and business analysis team is collecting on-chain data directly by running their own Ethereum archive node. They will need a method to sign operations and include them in documents, with them being responsible for designing their document models. Dracaena - Powerhouse anticipates spending two days a week assisting the team with this work.
Meeting Schedule and Planning Dracaena - Powerhouse outlined the day's schedule, confirming that lunch would occur first, followed by breakout sessions. They proposed that the breakout sessions be about one and a half hours, with an additional half hour to bring everyone back together, before "putting the roof together".
Database Library Inquiry Dracaena - Powerhouse asked Frank about the library used for creating processor tables and adding columns in migrations, specifically the PG library. They confirmed the library name as Kaiser, noting it is an external package.

Summary
The BAI weekly call noted delays for DSpot's MVP finalization due to ongoing work by Kilgore and Draa on the Acra services billing costing add-on steps, while Teep provided Jasmine with feedback for builder profile pages, including adding an operator icon and a direct website link. Wouter and Libram discussed restructuring read and calculation functions into a new "queries" folder, with Wouter establishing that document models should use query functions for calculated values, taking document state and optional external parameters to avoid excessive recalculations. Wouter set a clear target for a Thursday User Acceptance Testing (UAT) with the RGH group, focusing on the end-to-end flow of creating and purchasing services on Acra, which requires Libram to finalize the updated `create product instances` mutation and push the latest calculated utils function.

Details
BAI Call Updates and Service Delays: The BAI weekly call was initiated, noting Aaron's absence and the brief update that their work involves meeting with Kilgore and Draa to finalize the billing costing add-on steps for Acra services. This ongoing iteration process is reportedly causing delays for DSpot in finalizing the MVP, which was originally targeted for the end of February (00:00:00).
Builder Profile Page Feedback: Teep provided feedback to Jasmine on the builder profile page, which aims to make the builder and operator profile pages as similar as possible in appearance. The plan is to add an icon, a hand and cog, to the builder list's team logo to indicate if they are an operator, and their profile page will then display the products they offer and an operator tag. Teep also mentioned adding a direct URL link, specifically a website link, to the profile page (00:01:17).
Finances Data Refresh: For the finances section, Teep noted that while they worked on getting the real data operational, the API needed refreshing, requiring them to reload data for snapshots and expense reports. Teep concluded their main product board updates, and Libram then mentioned their task of acting as a "firefighter" to make network queries more robust (00:02:21).
Service Offerings Mapper Function: Libram confirmed they would be working on a helper mapper function from the service offerings models, a task derived from a message passed by Aaron (00:02:21). Wouter noted that this function is essentially a utils exportable mapper function that maps the user-selected tiers to a payload for the `create product instance` query, which will be served to DSpot (00:03:39).
Calculated Values in Document Models: Wouter discussed the general pattern of calculated values within the document model, using the invoice document model as an example, which includes calculated values such as subtotals and totals (00:04:56). It was established that including all calculated values in the document state can lead to excessive recalculations and redundancy, especially when calculations depend on external parameters like timestamps (00:06:21). The preference is to include business logic within the document model via query functions that take the document state and optional external parameters (00:08:08).
Structuring Read Functions as Utilities: Wouter proposed that read functions, or calculation functions, should be bundled with the document model via the existing `utils` object (00:09:51). They advised a consistent structure for these functions: taking the document state as the first parameter and an optional `params` object (for external data like timestamps) as the second, ensuring the function remains pure (00:10:55). Wouter also suggested moving editor-specific logic into these util functions to make them accessible to external developers using the document model (00:12:09).
Refactoring Utils into a Queries Folder: To enforce the idea that read functions are a category separate from reducers (which mutate state), Wouter suggested creating a new "queries" folder next to the reducers folder for these calculation functions (00:14:09). Libram confirmed the current implementation uses the utils file as an exportable function that Acra front end can import to calculate the price breakdown based on state and user selection (00:13:12). The utility functions should be placed in the `queries` folder, and the main `utils.ts` file should serve only to compose the full util set (00:17:14).
Need for Document Model in Acra Client: Wouter inquired about the progress of using document models inside the Acra client without a React dependency, and Libram confirmed that this approach has not yet been tested locally or communicated to DSpot (00:24:02). Libram noted that core development advised against implementing a previously discussed class for submitting the document to the backend, citing the need for extra work (00:25:06).
Proposed Solution for Acra Submission Payload: Libram explained their proposed solution for Acra, which involves querying the service offering state via GraphQL and storing the resulting price breakdown, calculated using the `get user selected price breakdown` utility function, in memory. Upon user submission, this price breakdown payload is passed as a blob to the mutation, allowing the system to create the necessary instance documents (00:32:45). Wouter acknowledged this approach works for the MVP, as it relies on the system signing the document and creating the instances (00:36:55).
Avoiding External Configuration Updates: Wouter emphasized the importance of avoiding operations like `update final configuration` with large input values because such objects introduce consistency issues and should ideally be derived within the document model (00:41:09). Instead, simple user inputs (tier selection, billing cycle, optional service groups) can live outside the document model and be passed as parameters to the query function for dynamic price breakdown calculation (00:43:20). Libram acknowledged this requirement and committed to refactoring the existing implementation (00:47:03).
Simulating vs. Editing in the Editor: The conversation confirmed that the current editor matrix simulates what the user sees, rather than directly editing the document state (00:47:03). Wouter suggested that the editor should clearly distinguish between simulating user input and setting default values, which would constitute an actual edit to the document model (e.g., setting a default tier or billing cycle). The matrix that reads from the "final configuration" is currently using multiple `set final configurations`, which Wouter reiterated as an incorrect approach (00:47:56) (00:50:17).
MVP User Acceptance Testing (UAT) Timeline: Wouter concluded by asking about the timeline for user acceptance testing for the MVP, suggesting a handover meeting to prepare for UAT by Thursday's RGH call. Teep confirmed that this timeline is likely feasible, as the only remaining work is the services billing component discussed with Libram (00:56:15).
Scope of Work and Testing Requirements: liberuum indicated that the immediate focus must be on reviewing all installed packages, repositories on staging, and running tests, including edge case scenarios, to eliminate throwable errors like the "document not found" issue observed during the call. They emphasized the need to refactor, clean up, harden, and create correct error boundaries so that users do not encounter raw errors. Wouter proposed that the first user acceptance test should cover creating a new product and a new service offering and publishing them to the website by Thursday (00:57:51).
Service Offerings and Network Display Logic: liberuum asked how Acra displays service offerings and if they are tied to a network or a builder, noting that current implementation seems to require network admin approval to add a drive to the builder list before display (00:59:29). teep clarified that services are displayed outside of the network level, suggesting the system picks up all services independently of the network (01:00:37). Wouter, liberuum, and teep then tested the flow for creating a service offering, identifying naming inconsistencies and confirming that the correct editor should display service offerings, not resource templates (01:01:36).
Configuring Products and Service Offerings: The team worked through the process of setting a product facet, defining a product (e.g., "cloud service" with the entity "Vetra"), and then offering a service for that product with three tiers (01:03:41). They discovered that a service offering must be linked to an audience, such as "builders," to display correctly in Acra. After addressing this, they confirmed that the product was visible and available for purchase, although a detail regarding service configuration was still missing (01:05:27).
Target for Thursday User Acceptance Testing (UAT): Wouter set a clear target for Thursday's UAT, focusing on the end-to-end flow from the operator drive to the final request submission (01:07:44) (01:14:13). The UAT will involve the RGH group gaining access to the RGH drive, creating a product, defining a facet, defining service offerings, and then acting as a client to purchase those services on Acra, which involves selecting a billing cycle tier and optional service groups (01:09:13) (01:14:13). The team confirmed that the process of requesting service purchase (the `create product instances` mutation) should ideally return a link to the created drive, which will be temporarily displayed to validate the flow (01:15:22).
Operational Issues with Connect Editor Loading: teep raised an issue about the slow loading time of Connect editors, which can take around 30 seconds (01:09:13). liberuum noted that this is likely due to version 533 using the old sync engine. Wouter suggested that the long loading time for the editor is a separate issue, likely due to it being a development build and the use of the VIt module loader, which builds resources in the background; they noted that dynamic loading for editor modules is being worked on (01:10:53).
Production Environment Setup: liberuum mentioned that they are running the dev setup, `PH services app`, across staging and production environments, confirming that the loading issue affects all environments (01:12:07). Wouter suggested that the production environment will need an update to use pre-built packages instead of the V loader and asked if a migration to new infrastructure with Kubernetes, involving Frank, has occurred (01:13:07). liberuum confirmed that the meeting regarding the new infrastructure has not yet happened (01:14:13).
Final Step for UAT and Required Fixes: The final step for the UAT is submitting the request, which utilizes the `create product instances` mutation, although a recent update to the mutation by liberuum has caused an error that the builders need to address (01:14:13). liberuum stated they must push the latest calculated utils function to fix the issue and inform the developers on how to use it to populate the configuration object. teep was advised to hold off on informing the developers about the error until liberuum has finished updating the required mutation and query (01:16:28).

teep - Powerhouse will tell Jasmine about adding the URL for a website link to the builder profile page.
teep - Powerhouse will reread the data for snapshots and expense reports to refresh the API.
liberuum - Powerhouse will harden and make the network queries more robust.
liberuum - Powerhouse will start exploring the helper mapper function from service offerings models, which includes moving logic from the editor to a utils function, creating a 'queries' folder next to the 'reducers' folder to store calculation functions, and refactoring the logic for updating the final configuration in the editor.
liberuum - Powerhouse will test locally the exportability of the function for Acra to import the package and use the function.
Wouter - Powerhouse and liberuum - Powerhouse will discuss the status of the MVP with the core dev team later today to determine if a version will be available on staging by Thursday for user acceptance testing.
liberuum - Powerhouse will push the latest calculated utils function to be fixed and add a query to pass the right parameters.
liberuum - Powerhouse will run through all the used repos to refactor, clean up, harden, and create correct error boundaries to eliminate throwable errors.
Wouter - Powerhouse will ask a question about the editor loading with PH service up.

Applying audit checklist to knowledge vault Wouter stated the intention to use the audit checklist on the knowledge vault to migrate it to standardized architectural patterns.

Google Calendar Integration and Missing Environment Variables: liberuum - Powerhouse attempted to connect Google Calendar with read-only permissions and a backfill date of January 1, 2026, but encountered an error stating the environment lacked write connections for workflows. Google Console Redirect URL Troubleshooting: Wouter - Powerhouse explained that a redirect URL mismatch required manual configuration in the Google console. Alternative Reactor Connector Fix by acaldas: acaldas - Powerhouse intervened to ask if the reactor connection had write access and suggested creating a new connection using the first item option. Local Instance Performance and Data Volume Statistics: Wouter - Powerhouse demonstrated a local instance containing nearly 120,000 emails running on PG Lite without Postgres, highlighting that read queries remain instant and responsive under constant write pressure due to separated read/write stores and read models. Financial Runway and Team Structure Adjustments: Wouter - Powerhouse explained that product-market fit is progressing well, securing a financial runway until the end of 2027 for baseline costs and mid-2027 for business development and project work. Business Development Options for Departing Members: Wouter - Powerhouse detailed business development options for departing members utilizing the Acro limited company, offering either a 20% commission upon deal closure or deeper involvement in design and execution with separate line-item compensation.

Contributor Bounties and Official Software Contributions: Wouter - Powerhouse described how builders can publish applications on the Acra platform and contribute improvements back to the official software branch in exchange for bounties or increased relative shares of future license revenue distributed by the Power Apps Genesis Association.

Administrative Offboarding Details and Recommendations: Wouter - Powerhouse announced that formal termination notices will be sent out the following day, Gmail accounts will remain active for approximately another month to preserve budget before deactivation, and recommendations or project promotional materials will be made available for portfolios.

## Introduction

Powerhouse provides official Docker images for deploying your applications in containerized environments. This guide covers the available Docker images, how to use them with Docker Compose, and the environment variables you can configure.

Docker deployment is ideal for:

- **Production environments** that require consistent, reproducible deployments
- **Development teams** that want to share a common environment
- **CI/CD pipelines** that need automated testing and deployment
- **Cloud platforms** like AWS ECS, Google Cloud Run, or Kubernetes

:::tip[Deployment Options]
This guide covers **Docker-based deployment**. If you prefer **traditional VM/server deployment** with direct installation, see the [Setup Environment Guide](./03-SetupEnvironment.md).

**Choose Docker if:** You want the fastest path to production, prefer containerized workflows, or are deploying to cloud platforms.
**Choose Direct Installation if:** You need maximum performance, want full control, or are setting up a dedicated server.
:::

## Available Docker Images

Powerhouse publishes three official Docker images to the Vetra Harbor registry (`cr.vetra.io`):

### 1. Connect

The Connect image provides the Powerhouse web application frontend with an embedded Nginx server.

```
cr.vetra.io/powerhouse-inc-powerhouse/connect
```

**Available tags:**

- `latest` - Latest stable release
- `dev` - Development builds (from `main`)
- `staging` - Staging builds
- `rc` - Release candidates
- `vX.Y.Z` - Specific version tags (e.g., `v6.2.1`)

### 2. Switchboard

The Switchboard image provides the backend API server that handles document synchronization and GraphQL endpoints.

```
cr.vetra.io/powerhouse-inc-powerhouse/switchboard
```

**Available tags:**

- `latest` - Latest stable release
- `dev` - Development builds (from `main`)
- `staging` - Staging builds
- `rc` - Release candidates
- `vX.Y.Z` - Specific version tags (e.g., `v6.2.1`)

### 3. Academy

The Academy image provides the documentation website.

```
cr.vetra.io/powerhouse-inc-powerhouse/academy
```

**Available tags:**

- `latest` - Latest stable release
- `dev` - Development builds
- `staging` - Staging builds
- `vX.Y.Z` - Specific version tags (e.g., `v1.0.0`)

## Quick Start with Docker Compose

The easiest way to run Powerhouse locally is using Docker Compose. The repository ships ready-made compose files — `docker-compose.yml` (production, `latest`), plus per-channel variants `docker-compose.dev.yml` / `docker-compose.test.yml` (`rc`) / `docker-compose.staging.yml`, and a postgres-free `docker-compose.pglite.yml`. The default file:

```yaml
name: powerhouse

services:
  connect:
    image: cr.vetra.io/powerhouse-inc-powerhouse/connect:latest
    # Auto-connect the SPA to the local switchboard.
    environment:
      - 'PH_CONNECT_CONFIG_JSON={"connect":{"drives":{"defaultDrives":[{"url":"http://localhost:4000","name":null,"icon":null}]}}}'
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:3000:3001"
    networks:
      - powerhouse_network
    hostname: connect.powerhouse
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "wget", "-q", "--spider", "http://127.0.0.1:3001/health"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 3s
      start_period: 10s
      retries: 3

  switchboard:
    image: cr.vetra.io/powerhouse-inc-powerhouse/switchboard:latest
    environment:
      # Reactor storage + entrypoint migration gate.
      - PH_REACTOR_DATABASE_URL=postgres://postgres:postgres@postgres:5432/postgres
      # Read-model storage. Both point at the same database.
      - PH_SWITCHBOARD_DATABASE_URL=postgres://postgres:postgres@postgres:5432/postgres
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:4000:3000"
    networks:
      - powerhouse_network
    hostname: switchboard.powerhouse
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://127.0.0.1:3000/health"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 3s
      start_period: 30s
      retries: 3

  postgres:
    image: postgres:16.1
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:5444:5432"
    environment:
      - POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres
      - POSTGRES_DB=postgres
      - POSTGRES_USER=postgres
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    networks:
      - powerhouse_network
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 3

networks:
  powerhouse_network:

volumes:
  postgres_data:
```

### Running the Stack

Start all services:

```bash
docker compose up -d
```

View logs:

```bash
docker compose logs -f
```

Stop all services:

```bash
docker compose down
```

After starting, you can access:

- **Connect**: http://localhost:3000
- **Switchboard**: http://localhost:4000

## Configuring Connect at runtime

Connect's runtime behavior is driven by `powerhouse.config.json` (the same file the build uses). For a Docker deployment you have three options:

1. **Mount your own `powerhouse.config.json`** as a Kubernetes ConfigMap / Secret (or a bind-mounted file) at `/var/www/html/project/powerhouse.config.json`. The SPA fetches it from `/powerhouse.config.json` on every page load, so post-deploy edits are visible after a refresh.
2. **Pass a JSON payload via the `PH_CONNECT_CONFIG_JSON` env var**. The entrypoint deep-merges it into the dist `powerhouse.config.json` at container start (operator-wins — concrete values in the payload override the baked file).
3. **Edit the file at build time** via `ph connect build --json '{...}'` or individual `--flag`s, baking the values into the image.

For the full configuration model, precedence ladder, and the complete list of `connect.*` fields, see the [Configure Environment](./04-ConfigureEnvironment.md) guide.

### Connect container env vars

Connect's SPA reads runtime configuration from `/powerhouse.config.json`, never from env vars at runtime. The container entrypoint, however, can apply operator-supplied JSON to that file at startup (operator-wins) — equivalent to pre-running `ph connect config --json '{...}'` on the dist file. The SPA then reads the file as usual.

#### Container shape and secrets

| Variable                 | Description                                                 | Default  |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------- | -------- |
| `PORT`                   | Port the nginx server listens on                            | `3001`   |
| `PH_CONNECT_BASE_PATH`   | nginx base URL path                                         | `/`      |
| `PH_CONNECT_CONFIG_JSON` | Runtime config JSON to merge into the dist file (see below) | _unset_  |

Connect does **not** read any database variables — it is a static frontend. Database connection strings belong on the Switchboard service (see below).

Sentry (DSN, environment label, tracing flag) is no longer set via per-field env vars — those live in `connect.sentry.*` of `powerhouse.config.json` and ride through `PH_CONNECT_CONFIG_JSON` like every other runtime field. See the example below.

#### `PH_CONNECT_CONFIG_JSON` (operator-wins)

Set this env var to a JSON object that mirrors the `connect.*` block of `powerhouse.config.json`. At container start the entrypoint deep-merges it into the dist file with **operator-wins semantics**: a concrete value in the env JSON overwrites the baked/mounted file; a `null` leaf (or an omitted key) keeps the file's value. Exception: `connect.app.basePath` is ignored — the base path is baked into the bundled asset URLs at build time (rebuild with `--base`, or use `--dynamic-base`).

```bash
docker run \
  -e PH_CONNECT_CONFIG_JSON='{
    "connect": {
      "app": { "logLevel": "debug" },
      "renown": { "url": "https://renown.staging.example", "chainId": 137 },
      "drives": {
        "defaultDrives": [
          { "url": "https://drive-a.example", "name": null, "icon": null }
        ],
        "sections": {
          "remote": { "enabled": true, "allowAdd": false }
        }
      },
      "sentry": {
        "dsn": "https://prod-key@sentry.io/1",
        "env": "prod",
        "tracing": true
      }
    }
  }' \
  connect:latest
```

The schema for the JSON object lives at `packages/builder-tools/connect-utils/runtime-config.schema.json` (also served as the `$schema` URL of any generated file). The same shape that `ph connect config --json` accepts is what `PH_CONNECT_CONFIG_JSON` accepts here.

**Invalid input behaviour:** malformed JSON or a non-object payload aborts container startup with a clear stderr message rather than silently dropping the operator's intent.

**Migration from per-field env vars:** the previous `PH_CONNECT_LOG_LEVEL`, `PH_CONNECT_DISABLE_ADD_DRIVE`, `PH_CONNECT_RENOWN_URL`, `PH_CONNECT_DEFAULT_DRIVES_URL`, `PH_CONNECT_SENTRY_DSN`, `PH_CONNECT_SENTRY_ENV`, `PH_CONNECT_SENTRY_TRACING_ENABLED`, and similar per-field variables are no longer wired. Wrap their values into a single `PH_CONNECT_CONFIG_JSON` payload using the JSON paths shown above. The Sentry **release** tag is build-time only — it stamps into the bundle via Vite's `define` from `WORKSPACE_VERSION` so it always matches the sourcemap upload tag CI used.

### Switchboard Environment Variables

#### Storage (Postgres or embedded PGlite)

Switchboard stores the reactor and the read models in one of two backends. When a Postgres URL is set it uses Postgres; otherwise it falls back to its embedded **PGlite** storage (local directories `./.ph/reactor-storage` and `.ph/read-storage` relative to the working directory — persist that directory with a volume, as the repo's `docker-compose.pglite.yml` does).

| Variable                      | Description                                                                    | Default           |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------- |
| `PH_REACTOR_DATABASE_URL`     | Postgres URL for reactor storage; also triggers the entrypoint's migrations    | _unset_ (PGlite)  |
| `PH_SWITCHBOARD_DATABASE_URL` | Postgres URL for the read model and (as fallback) the reactor                  | _unset_ (PGlite)  |
| `DATABASE_URL`                | Postgres URL for the read model (checked before `PH_SWITCHBOARD_DATABASE_URL`) | _unset_ (PGlite)  |

For a single-database deployment (the normal case, and what the repo's compose files do), set `PH_REACTOR_DATABASE_URL` and `PH_SWITCHBOARD_DATABASE_URL` to the same URL.

| Variable              | Description                                                                    | Default  |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------- |
| `PH_PGLITE_IN_MEMORY` | `1` = run PGlite in memory (no persistence)                                    | _unset_  |
| `PH_MIGRATE_PGLITE`   | `true` = migrate local PGlite data to the PG version this image ships          | _unset_  |
| `PH_FORCE_PG_VERSION` | `16` or `17` = wipe the local PGlite data dirs and re-initialize at that major | _unset_  |
| `SKIP_DB_MIGRATIONS`  | `true` = skip the entrypoint's Postgres migration run                          | _unset_  |

#### Core Configuration

| Variable                    | Description                                                          | Default                     |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------   | -------------------------   |
| `PORT`                      | Port the server listens on (exported as `PH_SWITCHBOARD_PORT`)       | `3000`                      |
| `PH_SWITCHBOARD_PORT`       | Explicit port override                                               | `$PORT`                     |
| `PH_DEFAULT_DRIVE_TYPE`     | `powerhouse/document-drive` or `powerhouse/reactor-drive`            | _unset_                     |
| `PH_PACKAGES`               | Comma-separated packages installed via pnpm at startup               | `""`                        |
| `PH_REGISTRY_PACKAGES`      | Comma-separated packages loaded over HTTP from the registry at start | `""`                        |
| `PH_REGISTRY_URL`           | Package registry base URL for HTTP package loading                   | `https://registry.vetra.io` |
| `PH_SWITCHBOARD_PUBLIC_URL` | Public origin used for the remote attachment service                 | `http://localhost:$PORT`    |
| `LOG_LEVEL`                 | Log level                                                            | `info`                      |

#### Error Tracking & Monitoring

| Variable                   | Description                                            | Default |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | ------- |
| `SENTRY_DSN`               | Sentry DSN for error tracking                          | `""`    |
| `SENTRY_ENV`               | Sentry environment name (e.g. "production", "staging") | `""`    |
| `SENTRY_TRACING_ENABLED`   | `false` = errors-only Sentry mode (no tracing)         | _unset_ |
| `TEMPO_ENDPOINT`           | OTLP HTTP endpoint for trace export (Grafana Tempo)    | `""`    |
| `PYROSCOPE_SERVER_ADDRESS` | Pyroscope server address for performance profiling     | `""`    |

## Installing Custom Packages

The two images load custom packages differently, matching where they run:

- **Connect** loads packages **in the browser at runtime** from the package registry. The registry base URL is the top-level `packageRegistryUrl` field of `powerhouse.config.json` (baked in at image build time). To use different packages or a different registry in a deployment, override those top-level fields with `PH_CONNECT_CONFIG_JSON`, e.g.:

  ```bash
  PH_CONNECT_CONFIG_JSON='{"packageRegistryUrl":"https://registry.example","packages":[{"name":"@powerhousedao/todo-demo-package","version":"1.0.0"}]}'
  ```

- **Switchboard** loads packages **server-side at startup**, in one of two ways:
  - `PH_PACKAGES` — comma-separated packages installed from the npm registry via pnpm before start.
  - `PH_REGISTRY_PACKAGES` — comma-separated packages loaded over HTTP from `PH_REGISTRY_URL` at start.

  ```yaml
  services:
    switchboard:
      image: cr.vetra.io/powerhouse-inc-powerhouse/switchboard:dev
      environment:
        - PH_PACKAGES=@powerhousedao/todo-demo-package,@powerhousedao/another-package
  ```

## Image Architecture

The images are built from a single multi-stage `docker/Dockerfile` (build args: `TAG` — the release tag, and `GIT_SHA`). A shared base stage installs `ph-cmd` for the matching release channel and initializes a project; each target then builds what it needs.

### Connect Image

The Connect target is **nginx:alpine** serving the static SPA — the frontend is built at **image build time** (`ph connect build`), not at container start. It runs as the non-root `nginx` user (UID 101), so pods can set `runAsNonRoot: true`.

At startup, the entrypoint script:

1. Renders the nginx config from `nginx.conf.template` via envsubst (`PORT`, `PH_CONNECT_BASE_PATH`)
2. Deep-merges `PH_CONNECT_CONFIG_JSON` into the dist `powerhouse.config.json` (operator-wins)
3. Re-syncs the Content-Security-Policy registry origin in `index.html` to the effective `packageRegistryUrl`
4. Validates the config (`nginx -t`) and starts nginx

### Switchboard Image

The Switchboard target is **Node.js 24 (Alpine)** with pnpm and the `@powerhousedao/switchboard` package installed at image build time from the npm registry at the requested release tag.

At startup, the entrypoint script:

1. Installs any packages listed in `PH_PACKAGES` (pnpm)
2. Runs the reactor Postgres migrations (Kysely) if `PH_REACTOR_DATABASE_URL` points at a Postgres URL — PGlite migrations run automatically inside the server
3. Starts the Switchboard server via Node.js

## Production Considerations

### Using Specific Version Tags

For production deployments, always use specific version tags instead of the floating `latest` / `dev` / `rc` / `staging` tags:

```yaml
services:
  connect:
    image: cr.vetra.io/powerhouse-inc-powerhouse/connect:v6.2.1
  switchboard:
    image: cr.vetra.io/powerhouse-inc-powerhouse/switchboard:v6.2.1
```

### Database Persistence

For production, ensure your PostgreSQL data is persisted using volumes:

```yaml
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16.1
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    environment:
      - POSTGRES_PASSWORD=your-secure-password
      - POSTGRES_DB=powerhouse
      - POSTGRES_USER=powerhouse

volumes:
  postgres_data:
```

### Health Checks

The provided compose files include health checks for all services: PostgreSQL (`pg_isready`), Connect (`/health` on nginx), and Switchboard (`/health` on the API). Switchboard only starts after the database is healthy, preventing connection errors during startup.

### Network Security

The example configuration binds ports to `127.0.0.1` only:

```yaml
ports:
  - "127.0.0.1:3000:3001"
```

This prevents direct external access. In production, use a reverse proxy (like Nginx or Traefik) to:

- Terminate SSL/TLS
- Handle load balancing
- Provide additional security headers

### Environment File

For better security, use a `.env` file instead of hardcoding credentials:

```bash
# .env
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=your-secure-password
PH_REACTOR_DATABASE_URL=postgres://powerhouse:your-secure-password@postgres:5432/powerhouse
PH_SWITCHBOARD_DATABASE_URL=postgres://powerhouse:your-secure-password@postgres:5432/powerhouse
```

```yaml
services:
  switchboard:
    image: cr.vetra.io/powerhouse-inc-powerhouse/switchboard:latest
    env_file:
      - .env
```

## Troubleshooting

### Container Won't Start

Check the logs for errors:

```bash
docker compose logs connect
docker compose logs switchboard
```

### Database Connection Issues

Ensure the database is ready before services start:

```bash
docker compose logs postgres
```

Verify the `PH_REACTOR_DATABASE_URL` / `PH_SWITCHBOARD_DATABASE_URL` format:

```
postgres://user:password@host:port/database
```

### Package Installation Fails

If custom packages fail to install, check:

1. Package name is correct
2. Network connectivity from container
3. Container has access to npm registry

### Permission Issues

The Connect container runs as the non-root `nginx` user (UID 101). If you bind-mount files or volumes into it, make sure they are readable by UID 101:

```bash
# Fix ownership for a bind-mounted Connect config
sudo chown -R 101:101 ./my-config
```

Switchboard runs as root, so host-side volume permissions are less restrictive there.

## Building Custom Images

You can extend the official images for custom deployments:

```dockerfile
# Switchboard: add server-side packages at build time
FROM cr.vetra.io/powerhouse-inc-powerhouse/switchboard:latest
RUN pnpm add --shamefully-hoist @powerhousedao/my-custom-package
```

```dockerfile
# Connect: the image is plain nginx serving the pre-built SPA (no Node.js,
# no ph CLI). Customization means overriding the runtime config via
# PH_CONNECT_CONFIG_JSON at deploy time, or swapping the served files/config:
FROM cr.vetra.io/powerhouse-inc-powerhouse/connect:latest
COPY my-nginx.conf.template /etc/nginx/nginx.conf.template
```

Build and push your custom image:

```bash
docker build -t my-registry/my-switchboard:latest .
docker push my-registry/my-switchboard:latest
```

## Installation

```bash
# Install globally
npm install -g ph-cli

# Install as a dev dependency
npm install --save-dev ph-cli
```

## Quick Start

```bash
# Initialize a new Powerhouse project
ph init

# Start the development environment
ph connect

# Install required dependencies
ph install @powerhousedao/core

# Generate code from models
ph generate --interactive
```

## Commands

### `ph connect`

Starts Connect Studio, a development environment for Powerhouse. This command launches a local development server with hot-reloading and debugging capabilities.

#### Options:

- `-p, --port <port>`: Port to run the server on (default: 3000)
- `--host <ip>`: Expose the server to the network on a specific IP (e.g. `0.0.0.0` for all interfaces, or a specific LAN IP)
- `--https`: Enable HTTPS
- `--open`: Open the browser automatically
- `--config-file <configFile>`: Path to the powerhouse.config.js file

#### Examples:

```bash
# Start Connect Studio on default port (3000)
ph connect

# Start on a specific port
ph connect --port 4000

# Expose to network and enable HTTPS
ph connect --host 0.0.0.0 --https

# Open in browser automatically
ph connect --open

# Use custom config file
ph connect --config-file ./my-config.js
```

### `ph generate`

`ph generate` is a router; pass a subcommand to generate a specific
module type. See `ph generate <subcommand> --help` for the full option
list per subcommand.

#### Subcommands:

- `document-model` (alias `doc`) — generate from a `.phd`/`.json` spec
- `editor` — generate a document editor
- `app` — generate a drive app
- `processor` — generate a reactor processor
- `subgraph` — generate a GraphQL subgraph
- `migration-file` — generate migrations for a relational-db processor
- `all` — re-generate every module in the project

Most subcommands share these options:

- `-d, --document <path>`: Path to a document-model spec (`.phd` or `.json`)
- `--dir <dir>`: Existing module directory to re-generate
- `-a, --all`: Re-generate every existing module of this type
- `-x, --extract`: (document-model only) Write a `powerhouse/document-model` spec for each existing model into `specs/document-models/`

#### Examples:

```bash
# Generate a document model from a spec file
ph generate document-model --document path/to/model.phd

# Re-generate all existing document models in the project
ph generate document-model --all

# Generate an editor for a given document type
ph generate editor --name myEditor --document-type powerhouse/todo

# Generate a drive app
ph generate app --name myApp

# Generate a processor
ph generate processor --name myProcessor --processor-type relationalDb

# Generate a subgraph
ph generate subgraph --name mySubgraph

# Generate migration files for a relational-db processor
ph generate migration-file --processor myProcessor

# Re-generate everything in the project
ph generate all
```

### `ph install` (or `ph add`, `ph i`)

Install Powerhouse dependencies with support for global and workspace-specific installations.

#### Options:

- `-g, --global`: Install the dependency globally
- `--debug`: Show additional logs
- `-w, --workspace`: Install the dependency in the workspace (use this option for monorepos)
- `--package-manager <packageManager>`: Force package manager to use

#### Examples:

```bash
# Install a package
ph install @powerhousedao/package-name

# Install globally
ph install -g @powerhousedao/package-name

# Install in workspace (for monorepos)
ph install -w @powerhousedao/package-name

# Install multiple packages
ph install @powerhousedao/package1 @powerhousedao/package2
```

### `ph uninstall` (or `ph remove`)

Remove Powerhouse dependencies from your project.

#### Options:

- `-g, --global`: Remove the dependency globally
- `--debug`: Show additional logs
- `-w, --workspace`: Remove the dependency in the workspace (use this option for monorepos)
- `--package-manager <packageManager>`: Force package manager to use

#### Examples:

```bash
# Remove a package
ph uninstall @powerhousedao/package-name

# Remove globally
ph uninstall -g @powerhousedao/package-name

# Remove from workspace
ph uninstall -w @powerhousedao/package-name
```

### `ph list` (or `ph l`)

List all installed Powerhouse packages in your project with detailed information.

#### Options:

- `--debug`: Show additional logs

#### Examples:

```bash
# List packages
ph list

# List with debug information
ph list --debug
```

### `ph inspect` (or `ph is`)

Inspect a specific package for detailed information about its dependencies, configuration, and usage.

#### Options:

- `--debug`: Show additional logs

#### Examples:

```bash
# Inspect a package
ph inspect @powerhousedao/package-name

# Inspect with debug information
ph inspect --debug @powerhousedao/package-name
```

### `ph service`

Manage Powerhouse services with various operations.

#### Options:

- `action`: The action to perform (default: "list")
- `service`: The service to manage (default: "all")

#### Examples:

```bash
# List all services
ph service list

# List specific service
ph service list service-name
```

### `ph version` (or `ph v`)

Display the current version of the PH CLI and related information.

#### Options:

- `--debug`: Show additional logs

#### Examples:

```bash
ph version
```

### `ph help`

Display comprehensive help information about the CLI and its commands.

#### Examples:

```bash
# Show general help
ph help

# Show help for specific command
ph help <command>
```

## Configuration

The CLI can be configured using a `powerhouse.config.js` file in your project root. Here's an example configuration:

```javascript
module.exports = {
  port: 3000,
  host: false,
  https: false,
  packageManager: "npm",
  workspace: {
    enabled: true,
    root: "./packages",
  },
};
```

## Troubleshooting

### Common Issues

1. **Command not found**
   - Ensure ph-cli is installed globally or locally
   - Check your PATH environment variable

2. **Permission errors**
   - Use sudo for global installations
   - Check directory permissions

3. **Package installation failures**
   - Clear npm cache: `npm cache clean --force`
   - Check network connectivity
   - Verify package name and version

### Debug Mode

Most commands support a `--debug` flag for additional logging:

```bash
ph install --debug @powerhousedao/package-name
```

nodes.title: The drive-analytics README still describes InternalTransmitterUpdate strands, an interface the reactor replaced with onOperations before v6.2.2-dev.74
A package webhook URL is a flat /webhooks/<token> whose token record carries the package and the key, so the URL leaks neither and an unknown, malformed or disarmed token all answer the same 404
The Powerhouse Analytics Engine stores time-series as value-interval triples instead of value-time tuples enabling delta and interpolation queries
Paged read-model processing controls memory by releasing objects as each batch completes.
A load-aware priority controller can yield background read-model work to user requests.
Separating read and write stores with read models keeps read queries responsive under constant write pressure, even without full Postgres.
A synchronized inbox can bridge remote webhook receipt to local processing.
The processor host module is layered across three packages: IProcessorHostModuleBase in shared, the read client added by reactor, attachments added by reactor-browser and reactor-api
The relational processor spec names migration injection and a compromised processor as its worst cases, and answers them with per-project database isolation

Processor timing measures the wall-clock time a processor's queue awaited, not CPU, so one processor's busy time never exceeds the window while the sum over processors can, and its read time includes waiting for the store connection
Waiting for a write to reach READ_READY from inside a processor is an anti-pattern, because READ_READY can wait on that processor's own batch
Data Processing and CQRS
Time-bounded analytics queries can expose document-history edge cases.
Four analytics stores split by runtime: MemoryAnalyticsStore and KnexAnalyticsStore run everywhere, BrowserAnalyticsStore is browser-only and PostgresAnalyticsStore is server-only
PGlite-backed analytics is about 1.36x the time of Postgres on 600+ real queries, so the memory store is a genuine alternative rather than a toy
Processor deliveries are ordered only within one document's scope and branch, so a processor cannot rely on a referenced document having arrived first
Read models on another database handle are not fenced against a purge and can write a row for a purged document from a batch fetched just before the purge committed
V6 processors receive a flat OperationWithContext list via onOperations instead of grouped strands via onStrands
Processors derive read models by folding operations instead of re-querying the source document
Processors maintain derived read models by subscribing to the operation stream.
A processor must erase a deleted document's data itself by handling DELETE_DOCUMENT and PURGE_DOCUMENT, because the reactor erases only its own records
Powerhouse relational database hooks provide type-safe live queries backed by PGlite with automatic re-rendering on data changes
Safe-merge beats overwrite when re-syncing externally sourced documents.
A read model stays reliable when source edits flow into its copied fields.
IAnalyticsStore.subscribeToSource fires for any path at or beneath the subscribed prefix and supports mid-path wildcards
A subgraph resolver gets a write client only while a mutation executes: ctx.clients.write in a query or subscription throws WriteClientUnavailableError
One package plugs into all three tiers: the Reactor runs its reducers, Connect renders its editors, Switchboard runs its processors
Processors are materialised views over the operation log and can be rebuilt by replaying from zero
Analytics dimensions are explored top-down by setting a high level of detail and reading the available paths back before narrowing the select
A throwing processor is isolated and never retried automatically: it goes to errored and its cursor is held below the batch it failed
Processor boundaries do not have to match document-type ownership.
A synchronized local index makes federated content searchable without querying each source live.
operation error index must match the number of prior dispatches
Processors run only on the in-process reactor path — the SharedWorker path silently skips every factory
A drive's deletion stays owed to every processor that missed it, and is delivered alone the next time its factory is registered
Currency is a filter field on an analytics query rather than a dimension, so comparing two currencies means two queries whose results are labelled separately
Processors implement IProcessor with onOperations receiving OperationWithContext items filtered by document type, scope, branch, and document ID
A replayed operation carries the document's latest state by default, which can be newer than the operation; replayState chooses collapse, exact or no state instead
The analytics engine's Postgres-versus-browser store parity check is one query run by hand, not a CI gate, so a change to either store's SQL can drift without any test failing
Analytics dimension paths use slash-delimited hierarchies with LOD parameter controlling aggregation specificity across dimensions
A processor factory is invoked only once a drive container exists, so until a drive is created no operation reaches any processor
A factory registered after its drive exists still receives the drive's creation header, so slug- or name-selecting factories work after a restart; only a purged drive's header is minimal
Each processor has its own delivery queue and receives one onOperations call at a time, so a slow processor delays only itself
Processor delivery is at-least-once, except that a crash between two concurrently projected documents can leave the lower ordinals unreplayed
A processor parks through a tombstone-lookup outage instead of erroring: it stays active, holds its cursor below the batch and probes every 30 seconds
A drive's own deletion reaches every processor of that drive whatever its filter, as the last delivery before onDisconnect
RelationalDbProcessor.deleteDocumentRows erases only tables that carry a document_id or documentId column, so every table must record its source document
A RelationalDbProcessor drops its namespace on a drive's deletion only when the factory passed the drive id and no other drive shares the namespace
context.resultingState is the whole document serialized with each scope and the header at its top level, so the global state is JSON.parse(resultingState).global
startFrom applies only when no cursor row positions a processor: a restart keeps the persisted cursor, while unregistering releases it

In-process read-after-write stays job-based: READ_READY is set only after the pre-ready read models commit, so any read model an in-process reader relies on must be registered pre-ready or it silently breaks execute-then-read
KnexAnalyticsStore now writes and reads its naive timestamp columns as UTC, so series rows written earlier on a non-UTC host read back shifted by that host's offset and need a one-time manual UPDATE
Operational processors make cross-document search possible by projecting document changes into relational read models.
Drive analytics writes one counter per operation with four dimension paths, so a question like which files were moved last week is a dimension filter rather than a scan
Analytics stores accept a query logger and a results logger whose indices match, so an asynchronous query can be paired with its own result

Before the client split, document reads queued on the operation log's single PGlite lane behind every executor transaction, so under 9 writes/s their p95 rose from 46 ms to 115-206 ms while read-store reads stayed at 36-53 ms
Read models and sync depend on resultingState and a global ordinal in OperationContext, and DocumentView will not rebuild state from operations

Operation-index ordinals come from a Postgres serial, so a rolled-back commit leaves a permanent hole and, when several executors commit at once, a hole can be transient, so a read model can neither demand contiguous ordinals nor simply skip a gap
Vetra scaffolds a processor only once its document has a name, a type of relational or analytics, at least one document type, at least one of the switchboard and connect apps, and status CONFIRMED
A read model whose factory fails at boot is now logged and left out while the reactor starts degraded, as the processor manager already was, instead of crashing the whole Switchboard

A relational processor's per-drive namespace is not drive-scoped: every drive's instance receives each operation its filter matches from every drive, so each namespace holds rows for all drives' documents
Processors need full drive IDs when drive slugs are not unique.

Package HTTP routes need no manual cleanup because the host releases a package's whole scope when the package is replaced, removed or the host shuts down — unlike its webhook tokens, which outlive the package
Webhook tokens live in the reactor's relational store, so a key mints the same token across reloads and redeploys, any host in a fleet can serve any endpoint, and only revoke(key) retires one
A processor that keeps its read model in memory is silently partial after a restart, because its persisted cursor resumes delivery after the operations that built it
DocumentIndexer answers graph questions the document itself cannot: getOutgoing, getIncoming, findPath by BFS and findAncestors over the full graph

A switchboard paces processor catch-up against request load: PH_CATCH_UP_PRIORITY=dynamic, the default, moves between levels 1 and 6 by request p95 latency and event-loop delay, while 0 stops catch-up and 7 runs it flat out
Processors write only through dispatch, whose execute, createInDrive and deleteDocument resolve once the write is accepted, not committed

A relational processor can be unit-tested with @powerhousedao/shared/processors/testing: createTestRelationalDb for an in-memory PGlite, runProcessorMigrations for the namespace, and operationsWithContext or testOperation to feed onOperations, which codegen's starter processor.test.ts already does
A package's own HTTP routes are served under /api/<its npm name>/ through one IHttpScope per package, shared by its subgraphs as this.http and its processors as module.http
The package HTTP scope has no middleware: a route's auth, body handling, prefix matching and size cap are declared on its registration, so its behaviour is readable from one place
Processors run in the background on Switchboard, folding the operation stream into read models served over GraphQL.
RelationalDbProcessor provides a type-safe base class with per-drive namespace isolation and lifecycle migration hooks

After the first scaffold a processor's files, not its Vetra document, decide what codegen registers: it never rewrites them, never unregisters an app, and reads apps, type and document types back from the files

A package route requires a verified Renown bearer by default, yet on a host with authentication disabled a renown route serves anonymous callers, so a handler that needs an identity must check ctx.user rather than trust its auth setting
Document-model subgraphs expose namespaced mutations taking documentIdOrSlug plus a <Model>_<Operation>Input
The relational layer wraps PGlite in Kysely and turns a processor's schema into typed live-query hooks with automatic parameter memoization
Reactor metrics are derived from six event-bus events, so every counter and histogram is traceable to the event that produced it
Processors query indexed data via getReadModel<T>(name), which throws when the read model is not registered
The relational-DB processor design exists to stop every processor reinventing database setup, and it names sharing tables within a project as an explicit goal
GraphQL can expose processor-maintained relational data as an application query surface.
Subgraphs are modular components that extend document models with custom GraphQL queries, plain HTTP routes, external integrations and cross-document logic
Content-hash gating avoids paying for redundant AI extraction.
Cross-document listings benefit from materialized reads when their inputs and scale grow.
The document cache keeps three maps — document promises, batch promises and listeners — so useDocuments returns a stable reference and Suspense does not thrash
The PGlite integration keeps the database handle in global window state so every component shares one connection, with events driving reactive updates
Document calculations belong in pure queries rather than persisted state.
The analytics engine is a distributed time-series system split into a core interface module and per-backend storage modules for knex, pg and browser
The relational-DB processor spec describes an API the code no longer has: onStrands, InternalTransmitterUpdate, PowerhouseDB and packages/document-drive are all gone at v6.2.2-dev.74
Analytics are bounded by the data synchronized into their reactor.
A poll-only source imposes a freshness floor that may require changing the system of record.
Browser analytics is a React Query provider requiring a database name, and a processor's analytics store must be registered with the processor manager by hand
Analytics development depends on a settled document model and explicit requirements.
operation errors are recorded on operations not thrown to callers
The "*" wildcard in a ProcessorFilter is honored only in documentId
Operational events can feed query-optimized analytics and database state.
A durable read model can become shared infrastructure for search and export.
A processor's indexing logic can be tested against an in-memory database without booting the reactor.
Existing rebuild data can seed search without a separate content export.
RelationalDbProcessor extends IProcessor to project document operations into SQL tables with type-safe migrations and namespaced databases per drive
Custom resolvers list a drive's children via ctx.clients.read.getOutgoingRelationships(driveId, "child")
Consolidating model data before querying can shift work from request time to preprocessing.
Predictive automation depends on a queryable, persistent knowledge base.
A forwarding application can bridge Stripe webhooks into a subgraph that processes them.
Cross-document relationships call for relational processing.
Local live queries do not provide cross-platform live delivery.
